citations.quote:
Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

The real sequence space
$$\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)=\left\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|x_n|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with its canonical inner product and norm from
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]], is complete and
therefore is a real Hilbert space.

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be separable real Hilbert spaces with a continuous inclusion $H_1\hookrightarrow H_0$. Let $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$ be an orthonormal basis of $H_0$ that is a complete orthogonal basis of $H_1$, write $w_j=\|e_j\|_{H_1}^2>0$, and set $f_j=e_j/\sqrt{w_j}$, so $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ is an orthonormal basis of $H_1$. Let $(\xi_j)_{j\ge1}$ be independent real random variables on one probability space with $\mathbb E\xi_j=0$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$, and let $\lambda_j\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j<\infty$. Then
$$S_N=\sum_{j=1}^N\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\xi_j e_j$$
converges almost surely in $H_1$ and in $L^2(\Omega;H_1)$ to an $H_1$-valued Borel-measurable random element $S$, with
$$\mathbb E\|S\|_{H_1}^2=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j.$$
These norm-convergence conclusions use no choice axiom beyond the supplied probability space and variables. For the following Gaussian conclusions, assume in addition that each $\xi_j$ has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. Under the Axiom of Choice and countable choice, $S$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element in $H_1$. Its covariance map $C:H_1^*\to H_1$, transported to $H_1$ by the Hilbert-space Riesz identification, is diagonal in the basis $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_jw_j$, and these eigenvalues are summable. If $D$ is a Borel forward-map domain in $H_1$ and $\mathbb P(S\in D)=1$, then the law of $S$ is a prior on $D$. Under the Axiom of Choice there is $a>0$ such that
$$\mathbb E\exp\!\bigl(a\|S\|_{H_1}^2\bigr)<\infty.$$

Let $X$ be a specified real separable Banach or Hilbert parameter space with metric $d_X(x,x')=\|x-x'\|_X$ and its norm topology. Let $(Y,d_Y)$ be a metric data space equipped with a sigma-algebra $\Sigma_Y$, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth set, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map. Choose a Borel set $D\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $D\subseteq U$ such that the restriction $G:=F|_D:D\to Y$ is measurable for the trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. A prior on this forward domain is a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that $\mu(D)=1$. Its restriction $\mu|_D$, defined by $\mu|_D(A)=\mu(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$, is then a probability measure on $D$, and the induced data law is $G_\#(\mu|_D)$, defined by $G_\#(\mu|_D)(E)=(\mu|_D)(G^{-1}(E))$ for $E\in\Sigma_Y$. A Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu(D)<1$ is not a prior on this declared forward domain.

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$. For $\ell\in B^*$ define
$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of
$\ell$ to $C\ell$ and extends continuously to an injective map $i:H\to B$;
we identify $H$ with its image in $B$ and use the completed Hilbert norm
$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

The term *RKHS* here denotes this covariance-induced Hilbert space of shifts
inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

Assume AC. Under the hypotheses and notation of
[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], each $C\ell$ exists as a
Bochner integral; $Q$ is a finite positive-semidefinite bilinear form;
$N=\{\ell:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$ is its nullspace; and the induced map from the
completion of $B^*/N$ to $B$ is continuous and injective. Thus the definition
identifies a Hilbert space of shifts in $B$.

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.
Assume AC. Every Borel probability on a Polish space S is tight.

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian
law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, and let $H\subseteq B$ be its covariance RKHS. Define
$\operatorname{supp}\mu$ to be the set of $x\in B$ for which every open
neighborhood has positive $\mu$-measure. Then
$$\operatorname{supp}\mu=\overline H^{\,B}.$$

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

The real sequence space
$$\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)=\left\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|x_n|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with its canonical inner product and norm from
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]], is complete and
therefore is a real Hilbert space.

Let $H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ with its canonical real inner product, and for each $j\in\mathbb N$ let $e_j$ be the sequence whose $j$th coordinate is $1$ and whose other coordinates are $0$. Then $(e_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H$. For every $x=(x_j)\in H$, the truncations $\sum_{j=1}^N x_je_j$ converge in $H$ to $x$, and $\|x\|_2^2=\sum_{j\in\mathbb N}|x_j|^2$.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

derivations.claim: Group the positive terms by dyadic blocks. For each $m\ge0$, there are $2^m$ integers $j$ with $2^m\le j<2^{m+1}$, and each has $j^{-2}\le2^{-2m}$. Hence $\sum_{j\ge1}j^{-2}\le\sum_{m\ge0}2^m2^{-2m}=\sum_{m\ge0}2^{-m}<\infty$.

By [F10], the coordinate vectors are a complete orthonormal basis of $H$. Apply [F1] using step 1.1 under the stated AC and countable-choice assumptions [A1]–[A2]. This gives the centered Borel Gaussian law $\mu$ on $H$, with covariance operator eigenvalues $j^{-2}$. The domain is $D=H$ and the identity map is measurable, so $\mu(D)=1$ and [F2] makes $\mu$ a prior on $D$.

By [F5], every $\ell\in H^*$ has the form $\ell_z(x)=\langle x,z\rangle$ for a unique $z\in\ell^2$. The covariance operator supplied by [F1] in step 2.1 is diagonal under this Riesz identification. By the covariance definition [F3] and commutation of bounded functionals with the Bochner integral [F8], $Q(\ell_z,\ell_y)=\ell_y(C\ell_z)=\sum_jj^{-2}z_jy_j$; this sum converges absolutely by Cauchy–Schwarz and $j^{-2}\le1$. The well-definedness theorem [F4] supplies $C\ell_z$ and the quotient completion. In particular, applying the coordinate functional $m_j(x)=\langle x,e_j\rangle$ commutes with the Bochner integral by [F8], so $\langle C\ell_z,e_j\rangle=m_j(C\ell_z)=Q(\ell_z,m_j)=j^{-2}z_j$. By [F10], finite-support sequences are dense in $\ell^2$; each lies in the RKHS identified in step 3.1, so the RKHS is dense. The vector $x=(1/j)_{j\ge1}$ belongs to $\ell^2$ by step 1.1 but not to the RKHS, since $\sum_j j^2(1/j)^2=\sum_j1=\infty$. Therefore the RKHS is proper.

The hypotheses of [F7] hold: step 2.1 gives a centered Borel Gaussian, step 3.2 gives tightness, and AC and countable choice [A1]–[A2] are assumed. By step 4.1 the covariance RKHS has closure $H$, so [F7] gives $\operatorname{supp}\mu=H$.

For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of Standard normal and normal laws has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let
$$\mathsf E=((\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Equip the parameter set with a specified measurable structure $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **proper Bayesian model** based on this experiment consists of a prior probability measure $\Pi$ on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]) and a probability kernel $K$ from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) that represents the experiment:
$$K(\theta,B)=P_\theta(B)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta,\ B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Thus $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,B)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every data event $B$, as required for a parameter-measurable model ([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). The family of measures in a parametric model alone does not supply this parameter sigma-algebra or measurability condition ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

The word **proper** means that the prior is a probability measure. A sigma-finite improper prior is not a proper Bayesian model in this definition; fixed-data posterior normalizers for such priors are handled separately.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_X$, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Here $\mathcal B(X)$ is generated by the norm-open sets. Give $D$ the relative topology and Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and let $\mu_{0,D}$ be the restriction of $\mu_0$ to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. Assume $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ is generated by the order topology on the extended real line and $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is its trace on $(-\infty,+\infty]$; thus $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded. Let $\mathsf Y_0\subseteq\mathsf Y$. Suppose that for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the section $u\mapsto\Phi(u;y)$ is finite and continuous as a real-valued function on $D$ with its relative topology inherited from the norm topology. Suppose there is one Borel function $M_1:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, independent of $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, such that
$$
\Phi(u;y)\ge -M_1(\|u\|_X)\quad(u\in D,\ y\in\mathsf Y_0),\qquad
\int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\,\mu_{0,D}(du)<\infty.
$$
Define $\operatorname{supp}\mu_0:=\{x\in X:\mu_0(U)>0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$. Then for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the evidence $Z_\Phi(y)$ is finite and strictly positive, and the normalized fiberwise update $\Pi^y$ is a probability measure on $D$.

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Let $X$ be a specified real separable Banach or Hilbert parameter space with metric $d_X(x,x')=\|x-x'\|_X$ and its norm topology. Let $(Y,d_Y)$ be a metric data space equipped with a sigma-algebra $\Sigma_Y$, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth set, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map. Choose a Borel set $D\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $D\subseteq U$ such that the restriction $G:=F|_D:D\to Y$ is measurable for the trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. A prior on this forward domain is a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that $\mu(D)=1$. Its restriction $\mu|_D$, defined by $\mu|_D(A)=\mu(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$, is then a probability measure on $D$, and the induced data law is $G_\#(\mu|_D)$, defined by $G_\#(\mu|_D)(E)=(\mu|_D)(G^{-1}(E))$ for $E\in\Sigma_Y$. A Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu(D)<1$ is not a prior on this declared forward domain.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces, called the **parameter space** and the **data space**. Let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty set of **admissible truths**, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a **forward map**. For $x\in U$, the datum $F(x)$ is its exact observation. For $y\in Y$, define the exact solution set

$$S_F(y):=\{x\in U:F(x)=y\}.$$

The datum $y$ is exactly solvable on $U$ when $S_F(y)\ne\varnothing$.

Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $U$, meaning it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive; truths equivalent under $\sim$ represent the same recovery target. A **metric solution-class space** for $(U,\sim)$ consists of a metric space $(Q,d_Q)$ and a function $q:U\to Q$ whose image is all of $Q$ and such that $q(x)=q(x')$ if and only if $x\sim x'$. The loss between two target classes is their metric distance $d_Q$. Exact recovery of the truth itself is the special case $Q=U$, $q(x)=x$, and $d_Q=d_X$ restricted to $U$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) with positive cone $P$. For
every $a \in F$ with $a \neq 0$ we have $a^2 > 0$, where $a^2 = a \cdot a$. In
particular, every nonzero square is positive.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
(Nonnegative simple measurable functions) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure (Measures on sigma-algebras) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
(Measurable spaces and measurable sets). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

derivations.claim: The set $D=U=\{0,1\}$ is Borel and nonempty. The function $\mu_0(A)=\tfrac12\mathbf1_{\{0\in A\}}+\tfrac12\mathbf1_{\{1\in A\}}$ is countably additive: in a disjoint sequence of Borel sets each of the two points occurs at most once, so the sum of assigned masses equals the mass of the union. Also $\mu_0(\mathbb R)=1$ and $\mu_0(D)=1$, making it a prior on the stated domain by [F8]. The identity $F:D\to\mathbb R$ is measurable because every subset of finite $D$ is Borel, and it satisfies the forward-map interface [F9].

By [A1] and [F1], each $N(u,1)$ is a probability law with the displayed density; since $D$ is finite, every evaluation $u\mapsto N(u,1)(B)$ is measurable, so [F10] gives a probability kernel. By [F2] and [F3], Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite. The potential and likelihood are jointly Borel: for each of the two $u$ values their data sections are continuous, each singleton $\{u\}$ is Borel in $D$, and each preimage of a Borel set is a finite union of rectangles $\{u\}\times B_u$ in $\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ by [F13]. Thus [F4] gives a proper Bayesian model with the stated prior and sampling kernel.

The finite subspace $D=\{0,1\}$ is discrete: the open balls of radius $1/2$ about $0$ and $1$ isolate the two points, so every real-valued function on $D$ is continuous. For every $u\in D$ and $y\in\mathbb R$, $\Phi(u;y)$ is finite. By [F11], $(y-u)^2\ge0$ and $a\ge-|a|$ for $a:=\tfrac12\log(2\pi)$, so $\Phi(u;y)\ge -C$ where $C:=|a|\ge0$. The constant envelope $M_1(r)=C$ is Borel, and [F12] gives $\int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|)}\,\mu_0(du)=e^C\mu_0(D)=e^C<\infty$. Applying [F5] with $\mathsf Y_0=\mathbb R$ proves $0<Z(y)<\infty$ and propriety of the normalized update for every datum.

For any $u\in D$ and $y\in\mathbb R$, put $a:=2\pi$; since $\log a$ occurs in the real-valued potential, [F15] gives $a>0$. Put $b:=\tfrac12(y-u)^2$ and $c:=\tfrac12\log a$. By [F15], $\exp(2c)=a$. By [F16], $\exp(c)^2=\exp(2c)=a$; by [F18], $\exp(c)>0$. Thus uniqueness of the nonnegative square root [F17] gives $\exp(c)=\sqrt{2\pi}$, and [F18] gives $\exp(-c)=1/\sqrt{2\pi}$. Applying [F16] again, $e^{-\Phi(u;y)}=\exp(-(b+c))=\exp(-b)\exp(-c)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(y-u)^2}{2}\right)=L(u;y)$. The last expression is the displayed Gaussian density, so the likelihood and potential agree pointwise.

By [F14], integrate the likelihood section against the prior. Step 3.2 gives $L(u;y)=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$ for both atoms, so this likelihood evidence equals $Z_\Phi(y)$, the evidence established finite and positive by step 3.1. The two atom masses are $1/2$, so $Z(y)=\tfrac12L(0;y)+\tfrac12L(1;y)$. Each density value is positive and at most $(2\pi)^{-1/2}$, so this displayed evidence is strictly positive and finite; integrating over any $A\subseteq D$ and dividing by it yields the stated posterior weights.

Apply [F6] with parameter $u\in D$, prior $\mu_0$, dominating measure Lebesgue, and the jointly Borel density $L(u;y)$. Its evidence is exactly the $Z(y)$ computed in step 4.1, so the displayed $\Pi^y$ is a data-indexed posterior-kernel version. By [F7], changing its values on a data-marginal-null set leaves the conditional identities unchanged.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Here $\mathcal B(X)$ is generated by the norm-open sets. Give $D$ the relative topology and Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and let $\mu_{0,D}$ be the restriction of $\mu_0$ to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. Assume $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ is generated by the order topology on the extended real line and $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is its trace on $(-\infty,+\infty]$; thus $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded. Let $\mathsf Y_0\subseteq\mathsf Y$. Suppose that for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the section $u\mapsto\Phi(u;y)$ is finite and continuous as a real-valued function on $D$ with its relative topology inherited from the norm topology. Suppose there is one Borel function $M_1:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, independent of $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, such that
$$\Phi(u;y)\ge -M_1(\|u\|_X)\quad(u\in D,\ y\in\mathsf Y_0),\qquad \int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\,\mu_{0,D}(du)<\infty.$$
Define $\operatorname{supp}\mu_0:=\{x\in X:\mu_0(U)>0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$. Then for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the evidence $Z_\Phi(y)$ is finite and strictly positive, and the normalized fiberwise update $\Pi^y$ is a probability measure on $D$.

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Let $X$ be a specified real separable Banach or Hilbert parameter space with metric $d_X(x,x')=\|x-x'\|_X$ and its norm topology. Let $(Y,d_Y)$ be a metric data space equipped with a sigma-algebra $\Sigma_Y$, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth set, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map. Choose a Borel set $D\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $D\subseteq U$ such that the restriction $G:=F|_D:D\to Y$ is measurable for the trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. A prior on this forward domain is a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that $\mu(D)=1$. Its restriction $\mu|_D$, defined by $\mu|_D(A)=\mu(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$, is then a probability measure on $D$, and the induced data law is $G_\#(\mu|_D)$, defined by $G_\#(\mu|_D)(E)=(\mu|_D)(G^{-1}(E))$ for $E\in\Sigma_Y$. A Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu(D)<1$ is not a prior on this declared forward domain.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces, called the **parameter space** and the **data space**. Let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty set of **admissible truths**, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a **forward map**. For $x\in U$, the datum $F(x)$ is its exact observation. For $y\in Y$, define the exact solution set

$$S_F(y):=\{x\in U:F(x)=y\}.$$

The datum $y$ is exactly solvable on $U$ when $S_F(y)\ne\varnothing$.

Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $U$, meaning it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive; truths equivalent under $\sim$ represent the same recovery target. A **metric solution-class space** for $(U,\sim)$ consists of a metric space $(Q,d_Q)$ and a function $q:U\to Q$ whose image is all of $Q$ and such that $q(x)=q(x')$ if and only if $x\sim x'$. The loss between two target classes is their metric distance $d_Q$. Exact recovery of the truth itself is the special case $Q=U$, $q(x)=x$, and $d_Q=d_X$ restricted to $U$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) with positive cone $P$. For
every $a \in F$ with $a \neq 0$ we have $a^2 > 0$, where $a^2 = a \cdot a$. In
particular, every nonzero square is positive.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
(Nonnegative simple measurable functions) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure (Measures on sigma-algebras) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
(Measurable spaces and measurable sets). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

derivations.claim: The set $D=U=\{0,1\}$ is Borel and nonempty. The function $\mu_0(A)=\tfrac12\mathbf1_{\{0\in A\}}+\tfrac12\mathbf1_{\{1\in A\}}$ is countably additive: in a disjoint sequence of Borel sets each of the two points occurs at most once, so the sum of assigned masses equals the mass of the union. Also $\mu_0(\mathbb R)=1$ and $\mu_0(D)=1$, making it a prior on the stated domain by [F8]. The identity $F:D\to\mathbb R$ is measurable because every subset of finite $D$ is Borel, and it satisfies the forward-map interface [F9].

By [A1] and [F1], each $N(u,1)$ is a probability law with the displayed density; since $D$ is finite, every evaluation $u\mapsto N(u,1)(B)$ is measurable, so [F10] gives a probability kernel. By [F2] and [F3], Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite. The potential and likelihood are jointly Borel: for each of the two $u$ values their data sections are continuous, each singleton $\{u\}$ is Borel in $D$, and each preimage of a Borel set is a finite union of rectangles $\{u\}\times B_u$ in $\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ by [F13]. Thus [F4] gives a proper Bayesian model with the stated prior and sampling kernel.

The finite subspace $D=\{0,1\}$ is discrete: the open balls of radius $1/2$ about $0$ and $1$ isolate the two points, so every real-valued function on $D$ is continuous. For every $u\in D$ and $y\in\mathbb R$, $\Phi(u;y)$ is finite. By [F11], $(y-u)^2\ge0$ and $a\ge-|a|$ for $a:=\tfrac12\log(2\pi)$, so $\Phi(u;y)\ge -C$ where $C:=|a|\ge0$. The constant envelope $M_1(r)=C$ is Borel, and [F12] gives $\int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|)}\,\mu_0(du)=e^C\mu_0(D)=e^C<\infty$. Applying [F5] with $\mathsf Y_0=\mathbb R$ proves $0<Z(y)<\infty$ and propriety of the normalized update for every datum.

For any $u\in D$ and $y\in\mathbb R$, put $a:=2\pi$; since $\log a$ occurs in the real-valued potential, [F15] gives $a>0$. Put $b:=\tfrac12(y-u)^2$ and $c:=\tfrac12\log a$. By [F15], $\exp(2c)=a$. By [F16], $\exp(c)^2=\exp(2c)=a$; by [F18], $\exp(c)>0$. Thus uniqueness of the nonnegative square root [F17] gives $\exp(c)=\sqrt{2\pi}$, and [F18] gives $\exp(-c)=1/\sqrt{2\pi}$. Applying [F16] again, $e^{-\Phi(u;y)}=\exp(-(b+c))=\exp(-b)\exp(-c)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(y-u)^2}{2}\right)=L(u;y)$. The last expression is the displayed Gaussian density, so the likelihood and potential agree pointwise.

By [F14], integrate the likelihood section against the prior. Step 3.2 gives $L(u;y)=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$ for both atoms, so this likelihood evidence equals $Z_\Phi(y)$, the evidence established finite and positive by step 3.1. The two atom masses are $1/2$, so $Z(y)=\tfrac12L(0;y)+\tfrac12L(1;y)$. Each density value is positive and at most $(2\pi)^{-1/2}$, so this displayed evidence is strictly positive and finite; integrating over any $A\subseteq D$ and dividing by it yields the stated posterior weights.

Apply [F6] with parameter $u\in D$, prior $\mu_0$, dominating measure Lebesgue, and the jointly Borel density $L(u;y)$. Its evidence is exactly the $Z(y)$ computed in step 4.1, so the displayed $\Pi^y$ is a data-indexed posterior-kernel version. By [F7], changing its values on a data-marginal-null set leaves the conditional identities unchanged.

$$\mathsf E=((\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Equip the parameter set with a specified measurable structure $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). $$K(\theta,B)=P_\theta(B)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta,\ B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Thus $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,B)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every data event $B$, as required for a parameter-measurable model ([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). The family of measures in a parametric model alone does not supply this parameter sigma-algebra or measurability condition ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

The word **proper** means that the prior is a probability measure. A sigma-finite improper prior is not a proper Bayesian model in this definition; fixed-data posterior normalizers for such priors are handled separately.

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in A Dirac set function is a probability measure.
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

Let $X$ be a set. The **counting set function** on $\mathcal P(X)$ is

The fact that this set function is a measure, and hence deserves the name **counting measure**, is proved in [[prop-counting-measure-is-a-measure]].
For every set $X$, the counting set function $\#_X$ of [[def-counting-measure]] is a measure on $(X,\mathcal P(X))$.

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\Pi)$ be a measure space, let $L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$

$$A\longmapsto c\int_A L_y\,d\Pi$$
is a probability measure if and only if $0<Z<+\infty$ and $c=Z^{-1}$. In
particular, if $Z=0$ or $Z=+\infty$, no finite positive scaling makes the

$$S_F(y):=\{x\in U:F(x)=y\}.$$

The constant map $F(u)=0$ is a forward map on the nonempty truth set $U=D$ by [F12], and its restriction is measurable because every preimage is $D$ or $\varnothing$. For each $u\in D$, $Q(u,\cdot)=\delta_0$ is a probability measure by [F4], and every evaluation $u\mapsto Q(u,B)$ is measurable on finite $D$; hence [F7] makes $Q$ a probability kernel. $$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set. The **counting set function** on $\mathcal P(X)$ is

$$\#_X(E):=\begin{cases}|E|,&E\text{ is finite},\\+\infty,&E\text{ is infinite},\end{cases}$$

The fact that this set function is a measure, and hence deserves the name **counting measure**, is proved in [[prop-counting-measure-is-a-measure]].
For every set $X$, the counting set function $\#_X$ of [[def-counting-measure]] is a measure on $(X,\mathcal P(X))$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space (Measure spaces).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.

For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of Standard normal and normal laws has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

$f:\mathbb N\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb N} f\,d\#=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}f(n),$$
where the right side is the nonnegative extended series of

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. sigma-finite measure on it, and fix a data value $y$. Let
$L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ be a $\mathcal T$-measurable function. Define its
**evidence normalizer** by
$$Z_\Pi(y):=\int_\Theta L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Only when $0<Z_\Pi(y)<+\infty$ define the **fiberwise posterior update** by
$$\Pi_y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)}{Z_\Pi(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The definition makes no quotient at zero or infinite evidence. A prior is
**proper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=1$, as in
[[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]. We call a sigma-finite
prior **improper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=+\infty$; the formula also applies to
other sigma-finite measures. For an improper prior, $Z_\Pi(y)$ is a fiberwise
normalizer only; it does not by itself define a prior-predictive probability or
a conditional law.

When the data are described by a dominated experiment, the dominating measure
and its sigma-finiteness are as in
[[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. A family of pointwise likelihood
sections is not assumed to be jointly measurable in parameter and data; that
additional condition must be supplied separately whenever Tonelli is used.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\Pi)$ be a measure space, let $L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$
be measurable for a fixed datum $y$, and put
$Z:=\int_\Theta L_y\,d\Pi$. For a finite positive constant $c$, the set
function
$$A\longmapsto c\int_A L_y\,d\Pi$$
is a probability measure if and only if $0<Z<+\infty$ and $c=Z^{-1}$. In
particular, if $Z=0$ or $Z=+\infty$, no finite positive scaling makes the
fiberwise update a probability measure.

$$\mathsf E=((\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Equip the parameter set with a specified measurable structure $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **proper Bayesian model** based on this experiment consists of a prior probability measure $\Pi$ on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]) and a probability kernel $K$ from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) that represents the experiment:
$$K(\theta,B)=P_\theta(B)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta,\ B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Thus $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,B)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every data event $B$, as required for a parameter-measurable model ([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). The family of measures in a parametric model alone does not supply this parameter sigma-algebra or measurability condition ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

The word **proper** means that the prior is a probability measure. A sigma-finite improper prior is not a proper Bayesian model in this definition; fixed-data posterior normalizers for such priors are handled separately.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_X$, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Here $\mathcal B(X)$ is generated by the norm-open sets. Give $D$ the relative topology and Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and let $\mu_{0,D}$ be the restriction of $\mu_0$ to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. Assume $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ is generated by the order topology on the extended real line and $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is its trace on $(-\infty,+\infty]$; thus $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded. Let $\mathsf Y_0\subseteq\mathsf Y$. Suppose that for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the section $u\mapsto\Phi(u;y)$ is finite and continuous as a real-valued function on $D$ with its relative topology inherited from the norm topology. Suppose there is one Borel function $M_1:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, independent of $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, such that
$$
\Phi(u;y)\ge -M_1(\|u\|_X)\quad(u\in D,\ y\in\mathsf Y_0),\qquad
\int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\,\mu_{0,D}(du)<\infty.
$$
Define $\operatorname{supp}\mu_0:=\{x\in X:\mu_0(U)>0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$. Then for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the evidence $Z_\Phi(y)$ is finite and strictly positive, and the normalized fiberwise update $\Pi^y$ is a probability measure on $D$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces, called the **parameter space** and the **data space**. Let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty set of **admissible truths**, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a **forward map**. For $x\in U$, the datum $F(x)$ is its exact observation. For $y\in Y$, define the exact solution set

$$S_F(y):=\{x\in U:F(x)=y\}.$$

The datum $y$ is exactly solvable on $U$ when $S_F(y)\ne\varnothing$.

Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $U$, meaning it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive; truths equivalent under $\sim$ represent the same recovery target. A **metric solution-class space** for $(U,\sim)$ consists of a metric space $(Q,d_Q)$ and a function $q:U\to Q$ whose image is all of $Q$ and such that $q(x)=q(x')$ if and only if $x\sim x'$. The loss between two target classes is their metric distance $d_Q$. Exact recovery of the truth itself is the special case $Q=U$, $q(x)=x$, and $d_Q=d_X$ restricted to $U$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
(Measurable spaces and measurable sets). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
(The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
Order on the natural numbers, which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$, proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
(Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

Let $\mathbb{N}$ be the von Neumann naturals, with $0 = \varnothing$ and
$\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and let $<$ be the order of
[[def-nat-order]], so that $m < n \iff m \in n$ and
$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\}$ ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]).
Write $\approx$ for equinumerosity ([[def-equinumerous]]). Then:

1. for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ there is **no injection** $\sigma(n) \to n$;
2. if $m < n$ then there is no injection $n \to m$;
3. if $n \approx m$ with $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, then $n = m$;
4. $\mathbb{N} \not\approx n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$;
5. no natural number is equinumerous with a proper subset of itself: if
   $A \subseteq n$ and $n \approx A$, then $A = n$.

Claim 1 is the pigeonhole principle in its sharpest form, that $n + 1$ pigeons do
not fit injectively into $n$ holes; the other four are the consequences the
library actually quotes. Claim 3 says a finite set is equinumerous with exactly
one natural number, so "the number of elements" is well defined. Claim 4 says
$\mathbb{N}$ is infinite. Claim 5 says no natural number is Dedekind-infinite.

**Why this is proved here.** The next item on this page defines finiteness as
equinumerosity with a natural number, and the three size classes it introduces
are exhaustive by construction but mutually exclusive only because of claim 4.
Several later items also need claim 3 or claim 5. The principle is elementary and
belongs with the naturals, but it is about counting rather than about order, so
it is proved here, immediately before finiteness is defined, from induction and
the identification of the order with membership alone. Nothing below uses
ordinals, cardinals, or any later material.

derivations.claim: For each $m\in\mathbb N$, the initial set $E_m=\{0,1,\ldots,m\}$ has counting measure $m+1<\infty$ by [F1] and [F2], and $\bigcup_mE_m=\mathbb N$. Thus $\mu$ is sigma-finite by [F3]. By [F16], $\mathbb N$ is infinite, so [F1] gives $\mu(\mathbb N)=+\infty$.

The counting-integral formula [F6] gives $Z(0)=\int_{\mathbb N}\frac{e^{-n^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\mu(dn)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{-n^2/2}$. Its $n=0$ term is $1/\sqrt{2\pi}>0$ by [F8].

AC implies countable choice by [F5], so the normal-density interface [F4] applies: for each $n$, $N(n,1)$ is a probability law with the displayed Gaussian density. Since the parameter sigma-algebra is $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$, every evaluation $n\mapsto N(n,1)(B)$ is measurable, and the likelihood section $n\mapsto L_y(n)$ is measurable by [F15]; thus the sampling family satisfies [F13]. The map $F(n)=n$ on the nonempty admissible set $U=\mathbb N$ satisfies the forward-map interface [F14]. By [F11] this is not a proper Bayesian model with prior $\mu$, because [step 1.1] shows the prior mass is infinite.

For every $n\ge1$, $n^2\ge n$, so monotonicity of the exponential [F8] gives $e^{-n^2/2}\le e^{-n/2}$. Let $r=e^{-1/2}$. By [F8], $0<r<1$, and [F7] makes $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}r^n$ finite. Comparison of nonnegative partial sums now bounds the evidence series in step 1.2 by $1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}r^n<\infty$. Hence $0<Z(0)<\infty$.

Applying [F10] to $L_0$ and the sigma-finite measure $\mu$ gives the probability with singleton masses $L_0(n)/Z(0)=e^{-n^2/2}/\sum_je^{-j^2/2}$, as stated. Its fixed-data meaning and lack of a prior-predictive probability follow from [F9]; [F11] confirms that no proper Bayesian model is supplied by this prior. The function-space propriety theorem [F12] does not apply because its prior is a probability, whereas [step 1.1] gives $\mu(\mathbb N)=+\infty$.
