singular; $K_{XX}$ and $K_{**}$ may also be singular. If a prediction-noise
vector $\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ jointly independent of the process and
$\epsilon$ is added to $f_{X_*}$, with $R_*$ symmetric positive semidefinite,
the conditional mean is unchanged and
$R_*$ is added to the conditional covariance. The displayed kernel is a
version defined at every $y$; conditional-law versions are determined only
$P_Y$-almost surely.

For computation, the occurrences of $C^{-1}v$ mean solving $Cu=v$. Since
$C$ is positive definite, its Cholesky factorization and forward/back
substitution evaluate these solves without forming $C^{-1}$.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_X$, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Here $\mathcal B(X)$ is generated by the norm-open sets. Give $D$ the relative topology and Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and let $\mu_{0,D}$ be the restriction of $\mu_0$ to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. Assume $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ is generated by the order topology on the extended real line and $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is its trace on $(-\infty,+\infty]$; thus $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded. Let $\mathsf Y_0\subseteq\mathsf Y$. Suppose that for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the section $u\mapsto\Phi(u;y)$ is finite and continuous as a real-valued function on $D$ with its relative topology inherited from the norm topology. Suppose there is one Borel function $M_1:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, independent of $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, such that
$$
\Phi(u;y)\ge -M_1(\|u\|_X)\quad(u\in D,\ y\in\mathsf Y_0),\qquad
\int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\,\mu_{0,D}(du)<\infty.
$$
Define $\operatorname{supp}\mu_0:=\{x\in X:\mu_0(U)>0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$. Then for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the evidence $Z_\Phi(y)$ is finite and strictly positive, and the normalized fiberwise update $\Pi^y$ is a probability measure on $D$.

Let $T$ be the finite index set with state indices $s_1,\ldots,s_n$ and observation indices $o_1,\ldots,o_m$. Define $f_{s_i}=X_i$ and $f_{o_j}=(AX)_j$. Every finite linear combination of these coordinates is a linear projection of $X$, so it is normal by [F1] and $f$ is a Gaussian process by [F3]. For each fixed $y$, $\Phi_y$ is finite, continuous, and nonnegative on $\mathbb R^n$, and $(x,y)\mapsto\Phi_y(x)$ is jointly continuous. Therefore [F9] gives $0<Z(y)<\infty$ for every $y$, and [F8] defines $\Pi^y$. The likelihood density from [F7] is a positive constant independent of $x$ times $e^{-\Phi_y(x)}$; its constant cancels in the normalized update.

The vector $f$ is a measurable function of $X$, so [F4] and [F5] make $\eta$ independent of $f$. The observed covariance is $K_{OO}+\Gamma=S\succ0$ by step 1.1. Applying [F6] with test list $S$ and observation list $O$ gives the displayed Gaussian conditional-law version for every $y$.

Suppose $r=\operatorname{rank}(C_0)>0$. By [F2], write $C_0=U\Lambda U^T$ and represent $X$ as $m_0+L\xi$, where $L=U\Lambda^{1/2}$ and $\xi\sim N_r(0,I_r)$. Put $B=AL$ and $d=y-Am_0$. By the pushforward formula for $\mu_0$ and the likelihood in [F7], the density of the normalized update in these coordinates is proportional, for every $y$, to $$ \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12\left[\xi^T\xi+(d-B\xi)^T\Gamma^{-1}(d-B\xi)\right]\right). $$ This is a pointwise fixed-data calculation; it does not replace the all-data version convention in step 1.3.

Set $Q=I_r+B^T\Gamma^{-1}B$ and $h=B^T\Gamma^{-1}d$. Then $Q\succ0$, and expansion gives $$ \xi^T\xi+(d-B\xi)^T\Gamma^{-1}(d-B\xi) =(\xi-Q^{-1}h)^TQ(\xi-Q^{-1}h)+d^T\Gamma^{-1}d-h^TQ^{-1}h. $$ Thus the update in step 2.2 is the Gaussian law of $\xi$ with mean $Q^{-1}h$ and covariance $Q^{-1}$, so the update of $X=m_0+L\xi$ has mean $m_0+LQ^{-1}B^T\Gamma^{-1}d$ and covariance $LQ^{-1}L^T$.

Since $S=\Gamma+BB^T$, multiplication gives $QB^T=B^T\Gamma^{-1}S$, hence $Q^{-1}B^T\Gamma^{-1}=B^TS^{-1}$. Also $Q(I_r-B^TS^{-1}B)=Q-QB^TS^{-1}B=I_r$, so $Q^{-1}=I_r-B^TS^{-1}B$. Substituting these identities into step 3.1 yields $$ m_0+LQ^{-1}B^T\Gamma^{-1}d=m_0+C_0A^TS^{-1}d $$ and $$ LQ^{-1}L^T=C_0-C_0A^TS^{-1}AC_0. $$ These are exactly the mean and covariance in the Statement.

If $r=0$, [F2] gives $C_0=0$ and $X=m_0$ almost surely. This also matches the conditional version from step 2.1 and proves the rank-zero boundary. Thus the fixed-data update and the stated all-data conditional version have the displayed law in every rank case.

Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_X$, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Here $\mathcal B(X)$ is generated by the norm-open sets. Give $D$ the relative topology and Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and let $\mu_{0,D}$ be the restriction of $\mu_0$ to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. Assume $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ is generated by the order topology on the extended real line and $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is its trace on $(-\infty,+\infty]$; thus $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded. Let $\mathsf Y_0\subseteq\mathsf Y$. Suppose that for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the section $u\mapsto\Phi(u;y)$ is finite and continuous as a real-valued function on $D$ with its relative topology inherited from the norm topology. Suppose there is one Borel function $M_1:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, independent of $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, such that
$$\Phi(u;y)\ge -M_1(\|u\|_X)\quad(u\in D,\ y\in\mathsf Y_0),\qquad \int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\,\mu_{0,D}(du)<\infty.$$
Define $\operatorname{supp}\mu_0:=\{x\in X:\mu_0(U)>0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$. Then for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the evidence $Z_\Phi(y)$ is finite and strictly positive, and the normalized fiberwise update $\Pi^y$ is a probability measure on $D$.

derivations.claim: For $v\in\mathbb R^m\setminus\{0\}$, $v^TSv=(A^Tv)^TC_0(A^Tv)+v^T\Gamma v>0$, since the first term is nonnegative and the second is positive. Thus $S\succ0$ and $S^{-1}$ exists.

Let $T$ be the finite index set with state indices $s_1,\ldots,s_n$ and observation indices $o_1,\ldots,o_m$. Define $f_{s_i}=X_i$ and $f_{o_j}=(AX)_j$. Every finite linear combination of these coordinates is a linear projection of $X$, so it is normal by [F1] and $f$ is a Gaussian process by [F3]. Its covariance blocks are $K_{SS}=C_0$, $K_{SO}=C_0A^T$, and $K_{OO}=AC_0A^T$.

For each fixed $y$, $\Phi_y$ is finite, continuous, and nonnegative on $\mathbb R^n$, and $(x,y)\mapsto\Phi_y(x)$ is jointly continuous. The prior $\mu_0$ is a probability on the separable Banach space $\mathbb R^n$, and the envelope $M_1(r)=0$ satisfies $\int e^{M_1(\|x\|_2)}\,\mu_0(dx)=1$. Therefore [F9] gives $0<Z(y)<\infty$ for every $y$, and [F8] defines $\Pi^y$. The likelihood density from [F7] is a positive constant independent of $x$ times $e^{-\Phi_y(x)}$; its constant cancels in the normalized update.

The vector $f$ is a measurable function of $X$, so [F4] and [F5] make $\eta$ independent of $f$. The observed covariance is $K_{OO}+\Gamma=S\succ0$ by step 1.1. Applying [F6] with test list $S$ and observation list $O$ gives the displayed Gaussian conditional-law version for every $y$.

Suppose $r=\operatorname{rank}(C_0)>0$. By [F2], write $C_0=U\Lambda U^T$ and represent $X$ as $m_0+L\xi$, where $L=U\Lambda^{1/2}$ and $\xi\sim N_r(0,I_r)$. Put $B=AL$ and $d=y-Am_0$. By the pushforward formula for $\mu_0$ and the likelihood in [F7], the density of the normalized update in these coordinates is proportional, for every $y$, to $$ \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12\left[\xi^T\xi+(d-B\xi)^T\Gamma^{-1}(d-B\xi)\right]\right). $$ This is a pointwise fixed-data calculation; it does not replace the all-data version convention in step 1.3.

Set $Q=I_r+B^T\Gamma^{-1}B$ and $h=B^T\Gamma^{-1}d$. Then $Q\succ0$, and expansion gives $$ \xi^T\xi+(d-B\xi)^T\Gamma^{-1}(d-B\xi) =(\xi-Q^{-1}h)^TQ(\xi-Q^{-1}h)+d^T\Gamma^{-1}d-h^TQ^{-1}h. $$ Thus the update in step 2.2 is the Gaussian law of $\xi$ with mean $Q^{-1}h$ and covariance $Q^{-1}$, so the update of $X=m_0+L\xi$ has mean $m_0+LQ^{-1}B^T\Gamma^{-1}d$ and covariance $LQ^{-1}L^T$.

Since $S=\Gamma+BB^T$, multiplication gives $QB^T=B^T\Gamma^{-1}S$, hence $Q^{-1}B^T\Gamma^{-1}=B^TS^{-1}$. Also $Q(I_r-B^TS^{-1}B)=Q-QB^TS^{-1}B=I_r$, so $Q^{-1}=I_r-B^TS^{-1}B$. Substituting these identities into step 3.1 yields $$ m_0+LQ^{-1}B^T\Gamma^{-1}d=m_0+C_0A^TS^{-1}d $$ and $$ LQ^{-1}L^T=C_0-C_0A^TS^{-1}AC_0. $$ These are exactly the mean and covariance in the Statement.

If $r=0$, [F2] gives $C_0=0$ and $X=m_0$ almost surely. Reweighting a point mass by the positive likelihood leaves that point mass, while the displayed formulas reduce to mean $m_0$ and covariance $0$. This also matches the conditional version from step 2.1 and proves the rank-zero boundary. Thus the fixed-data update and the stated all-data conditional version have the displayed law in every rank case.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a specified real separable Banach or Hilbert parameter space with metric $d_X(x,x')=\|x-x'\|_X$ and its norm topology. Let $(Y,d_Y)$ be a metric data space equipped with a sigma-algebra $\Sigma_Y$, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth set, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map. Choose a Borel set $D\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $D\subseteq U$ such that the restriction $G:=F|_D:D\to Y$ is measurable for the trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. A prior on this forward domain is a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that $\mu(D)=1$. Its restriction $\mu|_D$, defined by $\mu|_D(A)=\mu(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$, is then a probability measure on $D$, and the induced data law is $G_\#(\mu|_D)$, defined by $G_\#(\mu|_D)(E)=(\mu|_D)(G^{-1}(E))$ for $E\in\Sigma_Y$. A Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu(D)<1$ is not a prior on this declared forward domain.

Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_X$, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Here $\mathcal B(X)$ is generated by the norm-open sets. Give $D$ the relative topology and Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and let $\mu_{0,D}$ be the restriction of $\mu_0$ to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. Assume $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ is generated by the order topology on the extended real line and $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is its trace on $(-\infty,+\infty]$; thus $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded. Let $\mathsf Y_0\subseteq\mathsf Y$. Suppose that for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the section $u\mapsto\Phi(u;y)$ is finite and continuous as a real-valued function on $D$ with its relative topology inherited from the norm topology. Suppose there is one Borel function $M_1:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, independent of $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, such that
$$
\Phi(u;y)\ge -M_1(\|u\|_X)\quad(u\in D,\ y\in\mathsf Y_0),\qquad
\int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\,\mu_{0,D}(du)<\infty.
$$
Define $\operatorname{supp}\mu_0:=\{x\in X:\mu_0(U)>0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$. Then for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the evidence $Z_\Phi(y)$ is finite and strictly positive, and the normalized fiberwise update $\Pi^y$ is a probability measure on $D$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random
element in a real separable Banach space $B$. There is a constant $a>0$ such
that
$$E\exp(a\|W\|^2)<\infty.$$
In particular, $E\|W\|^2<\infty$.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.
Assume AC. Every Borel probability on a Polish space S is tight.

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian
law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, and let $H\subseteq B$ be its covariance RKHS. Define
$\operatorname{supp}\mu$ to be the set of $x\in B$ for which every open
neighborhood has positive $\mu$-measure. Then
$$\operatorname{supp}\mu=\overline H^{\,B}.$$

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$. For $\ell\in B^*$ define
$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of
$\ell$ to $C\ell$ and extends continuously to an injective map $i:H\to B$;
we identify $H$ with its image in $B$ and use the completed Hilbert norm
$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

The term *RKHS* here denotes this covariance-induced Hilbert space of shifts
inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

Assume AC. Under the hypotheses and notation of
[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], each $C\ell$ exists as a
Bochner integral; $Q$ is a finite positive-semidefinite bilinear form;
$N=\{\ell:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$ is its nullspace; and the induced map from the
completion of $B^*/N$ to $B$ is continuous and injective. Thus the definition
identifies a Hilbert space of shifts in $B$.

Assume AC. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, and let $H\subset B$ be its covariance RKHS. The closed Hilbert
unit ball
$$H_1=\{h\in H:\|h\|_H\le1\}$$
is compact in the Banach norm.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, the Hahn–Banach theorem, and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space, and let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element with law $\mu$. Define its covariance by $C\ell=\mathbb E[\ell(W)W]$ for $\ell\in B^*$, let $N=\{\ell:\mathbb E[\ell(W)^2]=0\}$, and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/N$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=\mathbb E[\ell(W)m(W)]$. Let $i:E\to B$ be the canonical injection extending $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. For $z\in B$ and $r>0$, write $\overline B_B(z,r)=\{x\in B:\|x-z\|_B\le r\}$. Then for any $h_1,h_2\in E$,
$$ \frac{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} \longrightarrow \exp\!\left(\frac{\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2}{2}\right) \qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
The denominator is positive for every $r>0$.

Let $B$ be a separable Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_B$, and let $\Pi$ be a Borel probability measure on $B$. For $z\in B$ and $r>0$, write $\overline B_B(z,r)=\{u\in B:\|u-z\|_B\le r\}$ and $m_r(z)=\Pi(\overline B_B(z,r))$. A **strong small-ball MAP** is a point $z\in B$ for which
$$ \frac{m_r(z)}{\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)}\longrightarrow1\qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
Assume AC for the covariance-induced Cameron–Martin notation. If $\Pi$ is a posterior law formed by weighting a centered Gaussian prior $\Pi_0$ on $B$, let $C\ell=\int_B\ell(u)u\,\Pi_0(du)$ be its covariance operator and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/\ker C$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=m(C\ell)$; the canonical injection $i:E\to B$ extends $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. A **Cameron–Martin ratio mode** is a point $ih\in iE$ such that, for every $k\in E$, the denominator is positive for all sufficiently small $r$ and
$$ \lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{m_r(ih)}{m_r(ik)} $$
exists and is at least $1$. This pairwise comparison over fixed Cameron–Martin centers does not assert the global strong small-ball MAP condition.

For every $r>0$, $\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)>0$: a countable dense subset gives a countable cover of $B$ by radius-$r$ open balls, each contained in its corresponding closed ball, and countable subadditivity rules out all such closed balls having zero probability.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

derivations.claim:
Choose $0<\varepsilon<a$ with $a$ from [F3]. The lower bound gives $\Phi(u)\ge M_\varepsilon-\varepsilon\|u\|_B^2$. Define the nonnegative Borel function $M_1(t)=\max\{0,\varepsilon t^2-M_\varepsilon\}$. Then $\Phi(u)\ge-M_1(\|u\|_B)$ and
$$ e^{M_1(\|u\|_B)} \le 1+e^{-M_\varepsilon}e^{\varepsilon\|u\|_B^2}. $$
The right side is $\mu$-integrable by [F3]. Since $\Phi$ is locally Lipschitz it is finite and continuous on $B$. Apply [F2] with the single datum and $D=B$; the prior definition in [F1] makes $\mu$ a prior on $B$. Thus $0<Z<\infty$ and $\Pi$ is a probability.

Fix $h\in E$. Local Lipschitz continuity at $ih$ supplies constants $L_h<\infty$ and $\rho_h>0$ such that $|\Phi(u)-\Phi(ih)|\le L_h r$ whenever $\|u-ih\|_B\le r<\rho_h$. Therefore
$$ e^{-\Phi(ih)-L_hr}\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r)) \le \int_{\overline B_B(ih,r)}e^{-\Phi(u)}\,\mu(du) \le e^{-\Phi(ih)+L_hr}\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r)). $$
For fixed $h_1,h_2\in E$, divide the two integral bounds and cancel the common normalizer $Z$ in [F1]. The factors from the Lipschitz errors tend to $1$, and [F7] gives
$$ \frac{\Pi(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\Pi(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} \longrightarrow e^{\Phi(ih_2)-\Phi(ih_1)} e^{(\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2)/2} =e^{I(ih_2)-I(ih_1)}. $$
The denominator is positive for small $r$: [F4] gives positive prior mass to every open ball about $ih_2$ (since $ih_2\in iE$), and the likelihood is strictly positive and continuous there.

Let $C_i=\|i:E\to B\|$. If $E=\{0\}$, $I$ has the sole candidate $0$ and is minimized there. Otherwise $C_i>0$. Choose $\varepsilon<1/(4C_i^2)$ and use the potential lower bound to obtain, for every $h\in E$,
$$ I(ih)\ge M_\varepsilon+\frac12\|h\|_E^2-\varepsilon\|ih\|_B^2 \ge M_\varepsilon+\frac14\|h\|_E^2. $$
Since $I(0)=\Phi(0)$ is finite, $\inf_E I$ is finite and any minimizing sequence is bounded in $E$.

Choose a minimizing sequence $(h_n)$ in $E$ and, by [F9], pass to a subsequence for which $\|h_n\|_E\to L$. Its images lie in a fixed multiple of the closed $E$-unit ball, whose image is compact in $B$ by [F6]. Pass to a further subsequence with $ih_n\to v$ in $B$; compactness means $v=ih$ for some $h\in E$. For each $\ell\in B^*$, [F5] gives
$$ |\ell(ih)|=\lim_n|\ell(ih_n)| =\lim_n|\langle h_n,[\ell]\rangle_E| \le L\|[\ell]\|_E. $$
The classes $[\ell]$ are dense in $E$ by [F5]. For every unit $g\in E$, choose nonzero classes $[\ell_n]\to g$ and normalize them; then $[\ell_n]/\|[\ell_n]\|_E\to g$. Thus the normalized covariance classes are dense in the unit sphere, and the supremum of $|\langle h,[\ell]\rangle_E|$ over them is $\|h\|_E$. The displayed bound gives $\|h\|_E\le L$. Local Lipschitz continuity gives $\Phi(ih_n)\to\Phi(ih)$, and therefore
$$ I(ih)\le\lim_n\left(\Phi(ih_n)+\frac12\|h_n\|_E^2\right)=\inf_E I. $$
Thus $I$ attains its finite minimum.

By [F7], the posterior ball ratio for fixed $ih,ik\in iE$ is $e^{I(ik)-I(ih)}$. This limit is at least $1$ for every $k\in E$ exactly when $I(ih)\le I(ik)$ for every $k\in E$. By [F8], those points are precisely the Cameron–Martin ratio modes. The comparison is only over fixed centers in $iE$; no supremum over all $B$ centers has been controlled, so it does not establish a global strong small-ball MAP.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a specified real separable Banach or Hilbert parameter space with metric $d_X(x,x')=\|x-x'\|_X$ and its norm topology. Let $(Y,d_Y)$ be a metric data space equipped with a sigma-algebra $\Sigma_Y$, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth set, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map. Choose a Borel set $D\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $D\subseteq U$ such that the restriction $G:=F|_D:D\to Y$ is measurable for the trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. A prior on this forward domain is a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that $\mu(D)=1$. Its restriction $\mu|_D$, defined by $\mu|_D(A)=\mu(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$, is then a probability measure on $D$, and the induced data law is $G_\#(\mu|_D)$, defined by $G_\#(\mu|_D)(E)=(\mu|_D)(G^{-1}(E))$ for $E\in\Sigma_Y$. A Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu(D)<1$ is not a prior on this declared forward domain.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_X$, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Here $\mathcal B(X)$ is generated by the norm-open sets. Give $D$ the relative topology and Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and let $\mu_{0,D}$ be the restriction of $\mu_0$ to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. Assume $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ is generated by the order topology on the extended real line and $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is its trace on $(-\infty,+\infty]$; thus $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded. Let $\mathsf Y_0\subseteq\mathsf Y$. Suppose that for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the section $u\mapsto\Phi(u;y)$ is finite and continuous as a real-valued function on $D$ with its relative topology inherited from the norm topology. Suppose there is one Borel function $M_1:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, independent of $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, such that
$$\Phi(u;y)\ge -M_1(\|u\|_X)\quad(u\in D,\ y\in\mathsf Y_0),\qquad \int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\,\mu_{0,D}(du)<\infty.$$
Define $\operatorname{supp}\mu_0:=\{x\in X:\mu_0(U)>0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$. Then for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the evidence $Z_\Phi(y)$ is finite and strictly positive, and the normalized fiberwise update $\Pi^y$ is a probability measure on $D$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random
element in a real separable Banach space $B$. There is a constant $a>0$ such
that
$$E\exp(a\|W\|^2)<\infty.$$
In particular, $E\|W\|^2<\infty$.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.
Assume AC. Every Borel probability on a Polish space S is tight.

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian
law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, and let $H\subseteq B$ be its covariance RKHS. Define
$\operatorname{supp}\mu$ to be the set of $x\in B$ for which every open
neighborhood has positive $\mu$-measure. Then
$$\operatorname{supp}\mu=\overline H^{\,B}.$$

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$. For $\ell\in B^*$ define
$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of
$\ell$ to $C\ell$ and extends continuously to an injective map $i:H\to B$;
we identify $H$ with its image in $B$ and use the completed Hilbert norm
$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

The term *RKHS* here denotes this covariance-induced Hilbert space of shifts
inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

Assume AC. Under the hypotheses and notation of
[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], each $C\ell$ exists as a
Bochner integral; $Q$ is a finite positive-semidefinite bilinear form;
$N=\{\ell:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$ is its nullspace; and the induced map from the
completion of $B^*/N$ to $B$ is continuous and injective. Thus the definition
identifies a Hilbert space of shifts in $B$.

Assume AC. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, and let $H\subset B$ be its covariance RKHS. The closed Hilbert
unit ball
$$H_1=\{h\in H:\|h\|_H\le1\}$$
is compact in the Banach norm.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, the Hahn–Banach theorem, and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space, and let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element with law $\mu$. Define its covariance by $C\ell=\mathbb E[\ell(W)W]$ for $\ell\in B^*$, let $N=\{\ell:\mathbb E[\ell(W)^2]=0\}$, and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/N$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=\mathbb E[\ell(W)m(W)]$. Let $i:E\to B$ be the canonical injection extending $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. For $z\in B$ and $r>0$, write $\overline B_B(z,r)=\{x\in B:\|x-z\|_B\le r\}$. Then for any $h_1,h_2\in E$,
$$ \frac{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} \longrightarrow \exp\!\left(\frac{\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2}{2}\right) \qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
The denominator is positive for every $r>0$.

Let $B$ be a separable Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_B$, and let $\Pi$ be a Borel probability measure on $B$. For $z\in B$ and $r>0$, write $\overline B_B(z,r)=\{u\in B:\|u-z\|_B\le r\}$ and $m_r(z)=\Pi(\overline B_B(z,r))$. A **strong small-ball MAP** is a point $z\in B$ for which
$$ \frac{m_r(z)}{\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)}\longrightarrow1\qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
Assume AC for the covariance-induced Cameron–Martin notation. If $\Pi$ is a posterior law formed by weighting a centered Gaussian prior $\Pi_0$ on $B$, let $C\ell=\int_B\ell(u)u\,\Pi_0(du)$ be its covariance operator and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/\ker C$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=m(C\ell)$; the canonical injection $i:E\to B$ extends $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. A **Cameron–Martin ratio mode** is a point $ih\in iE$ such that, for every $k\in E$, the denominator is positive for all sufficiently small $r$ and
$$ \lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{m_r(ih)}{m_r(ik)} $$
exists and is at least $1$. This pairwise comparison over fixed Cameron–Martin centers does not assert the global strong small-ball MAP condition.

For every $r>0$, $\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)>0$: a countable dense subset gives a countable cover of $B$ by radius-$r$ open balls, each contained in its corresponding closed ball, and countable subadditivity rules out all such closed balls having zero probability.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Choose $0<\varepsilon<a$ with $a$ from [F3]. The lower bound gives $\Phi(u)\ge M_\varepsilon-\varepsilon\|u\|_B^2$. Define the nonnegative Borel function $M_1(t)=\max\{0,\varepsilon t^2-M_\varepsilon\}$. Then $\Phi(u)\ge-M_1(\|u\|_B)$ and
$$ e^{M_1(\|u\|_B)} \le 1+e^{-M_\varepsilon}e^{\varepsilon\|u\|_B^2}. $$
The right side is $\mu$-integrable by [F3]. Since $\Phi$ is locally Lipschitz it is finite and continuous on $B$. Apply [F2] with the single datum and $D=B$; the prior definition in [F1] makes $\mu$ a prior on $B$. Thus $0<Z<\infty$ and $\Pi$ is a probability.

Fix $h\in E$. Local Lipschitz continuity at $ih$ supplies constants $L_h<\infty$ and $\rho_h>0$ such that $|\Phi(u)-\Phi(ih)|\le L_h r$ whenever $\|u-ih\|_B\le r<\rho_h$. Therefore
$$ e^{-\Phi(ih)-L_hr}\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r)) \le \int_{\overline B_B(ih,r)}e^{-\Phi(u)}\,\mu(du) \le e^{-\Phi(ih)+L_hr}\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r)). $$
For fixed $h_1,h_2\in E$, divide the two integral bounds and cancel the common normalizer $Z$ in [F1]. The factors from the Lipschitz errors tend to $1$, and [F7] gives
$$ \frac{\Pi(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\Pi(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} \longrightarrow e^{\Phi(ih_2)-\Phi(ih_1)} e^{(\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2)/2} =e^{I(ih_2)-I(ih_1)}. $$
The denominator is positive for small $r$: [F4] gives positive prior mass to every open ball about $ih_2$ (since $ih_2\in iE$), and the likelihood is strictly positive and continuous there.

Let $C_i=\|i:E\to B\|$. If $E=\{0\}$, $I$ has the sole candidate $0$ and is minimized there. Otherwise $C_i>0$. Choose $\varepsilon<1/(4C_i^2)$ and use the potential lower bound to obtain, for every $h\in E$,
$$ I(ih)\ge M_\varepsilon+\frac12\|h\|_E^2-\varepsilon\|ih\|_B^2 \ge M_\varepsilon+\frac14\|h\|_E^2. $$
Since $I(0)=\Phi(0)$ is finite, $\inf_E I$ is finite and any minimizing sequence is bounded in $E$.

Choose a minimizing sequence $(h_n)$ in $E$ and, by [F9], pass to a subsequence for which $\|h_n\|_E\to L$. Its images lie in a fixed multiple of the closed $E$-unit ball, whose image is compact in $B$ by [F6]. Pass to a further subsequence with $ih_n\to v$ in $B$; compactness means $v=ih$ for some $h\in E$. For each $\ell\in B^*$, [F5] gives
$$ |\ell(ih)|=\lim_n|\ell(ih_n)| =\lim_n|\langle h_n,[\ell]\rangle_E| \le L\|[\ell]\|_E. $$
The classes $[\ell]$ are dense in $E$ by [F5]. For every unit $g\in E$, choose nonzero classes $[\ell_n]\to g$ and normalize them; then $[\ell_n]/\|[\ell_n]\|_E\to g$. Thus the normalized covariance classes are dense in the unit sphere, and the supremum of $|\langle h,[\ell]\rangle_E|$ over them is $\|h\|_E$. The displayed bound gives $\|h\|_E\le L$. Local Lipschitz continuity gives $\Phi(ih_n)\to\Phi(ih)$, and therefore
$$ I(ih)\le\lim_n\left(\Phi(ih_n)+\frac12\|h_n\|_E^2\right)=\inf_E I. $$
Thus $I$ attains its finite minimum.

By [F7], the posterior ball ratio for fixed $ih,ik\in iE$ is $e^{I(ik)-I(ih)}$. This limit is at least $1$ for every $k\in E$ exactly when $I(ih)\le I(ik)$ for every $k\in E$. By [F8], those points are precisely the Cameron–Martin ratio modes. The comparison is only over fixed centers in $iE$; no supremum over all $B$ centers has been controlled, so it does not establish a global strong small-ball MAP.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be separable real Hilbert spaces with a continuous inclusion $H_1\hookrightarrow H_0$. Let $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$ be an orthonormal basis of $H_0$ that is a complete orthogonal basis of $H_1$, write $w_j=\|e_j\|_{H_1}^2>0$, and set $f_j=e_j/\sqrt{w_j}$, so $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ is an orthonormal basis of $H_1$. Let $(\xi_j)_{j\ge1}$ be independent real random variables on one probability space with $\mathbb E\xi_j=0$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$, and let $\lambda_j\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j<\infty$. Then
$$S_N=\sum_{j=1}^N\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\xi_j e_j$$
converges almost surely in $H_1$ and in $L^2(\Omega;H_1)$ to an $H_1$-valued Borel-measurable random element $S$, with
$$\mathbb E\|S\|_{H_1}^2=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j.$$
These norm-convergence conclusions use no choice axiom beyond the supplied probability space and variables. For the following Gaussian conclusions, assume in addition that each $\xi_j$ has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. Under the Axiom of Choice and countable choice, $S$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element in $H_1$. Its covariance map $C:H_1^*\to H_1$, transported to $H_1$ by the Hilbert-space Riesz identification, is diagonal in the basis $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_jw_j$, and these eigenvalues are summable. If $D$ is a Borel forward-map domain in $H_1$ and $\mathbb P(S\in D)=1$, then the law of $S$ is a prior on $D$. Under the Axiom of Choice there is $a>0$ such that
$$\mathbb E\exp\!\bigl(a\|S\|_{H_1}^2\bigr)<\infty.$$

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of Series in the nonnegative extended real line.

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The real numbers) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a family of at most countable sets
([[def-countable]]) indexed by $\mathbb{N}$. Then

$$U = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n$$

is at most countable.

**The role of $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.** It is spent at exactly one step, step 3.1 below, where a surjection $\mathbb N\to A_n$ is selected simultaneously for each nonempty $A_n$. The individual countability hypotheses assert that these sets of surjections are nonempty; they specify no simultaneous selection.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

derivations.claim: In [F1], take $H_0=H_1=\ell^2$, $w_j=1$, and $\lambda_j=1/(j(j+1))$. The finite sums telescope as $\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_j=\sum_{j=1}^N(1/j-1/(j+1))=1-1/(N+1)\le1$, so the required infinite sum is finite. Thus [F1] applies to the stated independent standard normals and proves that $W$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element.

Suppose that $\lambda$ is a translation-invariant Borel measure finite on every bounded Borel set. Put $U_j=\{x:\|x-e_j\|_2<1/3\}$. For $j\ne k$, $\|e_j-e_k\|_2=\sqrt2>2/3$, so the $U_j$ are pairwise disjoint. Each lies in the bounded ball $\{x:\|x\|_2<2\}$ by the triangle inequality. Translation invariance gives $\lambda(U_j)=m$ independent of $j$. If $m>0$, the first $N$ disjoint balls have total measure $Nm$ for every $N$, contradicting finiteness of the radius-two ball. Hence $m=0$.

Translation invariance and step 2.1 make every radius-$1/3$ ball have measure zero. Let $D$ be the set of finitely supported rational sequences. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be separable real Hilbert spaces with a continuous inclusion $H_1\hookrightarrow H_0$. Let $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$ be an orthonormal basis of $H_0$ that is a complete orthogonal basis of $H_1$, write $w_j=\|e_j\|_{H_1}^2>0$, and set $f_j=e_j/\sqrt{w_j}$, so $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ is an orthonormal basis of $H_1$. Let $(\xi_j)_{j\ge1}$ be independent real random variables on one probability space with $\mathbb E\xi_j=0$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$, and let $\lambda_j\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j<\infty$. Then
$$S_N=\sum_{j=1}^N\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\xi_j e_j$$
converges almost surely in $H_1$ and in $L^2(\Omega;H_1)$ to an $H_1$-valued Borel-measurable random element $S$, with
$$\mathbb E\|S\|_{H_1}^2=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j.$$
These norm-convergence conclusions use no choice axiom beyond the supplied probability space and variables. For the following Gaussian conclusions, assume in addition that each $\xi_j$ has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. Under the Axiom of Choice and countable choice, $S$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element in $H_1$. Its covariance map $C:H_1^*\to H_1$, transported to $H_1$ by the Hilbert-space Riesz identification, is diagonal in the basis $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_jw_j$, and these eigenvalues are summable. If $D$ is a Borel forward-map domain in $H_1$ and $\mathbb P(S\in D)=1$, then the law of $S$ is a prior on $D$. Under the Axiom of Choice there is $a>0$ such that
$$\mathbb E\exp\!\bigl(a\|S\|_{H_1}^2\bigr)<\infty.$$

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of Series in the nonnegative extended real line.

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The real numbers) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a family of at most countable sets
([[def-countable]]) indexed by $\mathbb{N}$. Then

$$U = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n$$

is at most countable.

The individual countability hypotheses assert that these sets of surjections are nonempty; they specify no simultaneous selection.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

> (Choice function).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$, let
$D\subseteq H$ be Borel with $\mu_0(D)=1$, and let
$\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be Borel. Assume the evidence
$$
Z:=\int_D e^{-\Phi_D(u)}\,\mu_0(du)
$$
satisfies $0<Z<\infty$. Extend the potential to all of $H$ by setting
$\bar\Phi(u)=\Phi_D(u)$ for $u\in D$ and $\bar\Phi(u)=+\infty$ for
$u\notin D$, and define the target probability
$\mu(du)=Z^{-1}e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du)$. For a scale $\beta\in[0,1]$,
write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$. At state $u\in H$, draw $\xi\sim\mu_0$
independently and propose $v=\rho u+\beta\xi$. Set the acceptance probability
to $0$ if either $\bar\Phi(u)$ or $\bar\Phi(v)$ is $+\infty$, and otherwise set
$$
\alpha(u,v)=\min\{1,\exp(\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v))\}.
$$
Draw an independent uniform random variable on $[0,1]$ and move to $v$ if it
is at most $\alpha(u,v)$; otherwise remain at $u$. The resulting one-step
transition rule is the prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson, or pCN, rule
$P_\beta$. States with infinite potential are absorbing under this total
definition; they have $\mu$-measure zero.

Let $X$ be a specified real separable Banach or Hilbert parameter space with metric $d_X(x,x')=\|x-x'\|_X$ and its norm topology. Let $(Y,d_Y)$ be a metric data space equipped with a sigma-algebra $\Sigma_Y$, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth set, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map. Choose a Borel set $D\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $D\subseteq U$ such that the restriction $G:=F|_D:D\to Y$ is measurable for the trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. A prior on this forward domain is a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that $\mu(D)=1$. Its restriction $\mu|_D$, defined by $\mu|_D(A)=\mu(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$, is then a probability measure on $D$, and the induced data law is $G_\#(\mu|_D)$, defined by $G_\#(\mu|_D)(E)=(\mu|_D)(G^{-1}(E))$ for $E\in\Sigma_Y$. A Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu(D)<1$ is not a prior on this declared forward domain.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_X$, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Here $\mathcal B(X)$ is generated by the norm-open sets. Give $D$ the relative topology and Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and let $\mu_{0,D}$ be the restriction of $\mu_0$ to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$. $$

$$
Define $\operatorname{supp}\mu_0:=\{x\in X:\mu_0(U)>0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$. Then for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the evidence $Z_\Phi(y)$ is finite and strictly positive, and the normalized fiberwise update $\Pi^y$ is a probability measure on $D$.

separable Banach space with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. A map

Borel-measurable and, for every $\ell\in B^*$, the real random variable

Borel probability $\mu=P\circ W^{-1}$. When the word *tight* is used, it means
that for every $\delta>0$ there is a norm-compact $K\subseteq B$ with

This definition concerns a random element in $B$. A Gaussian process on an
arbitrary index set with only a cylinder-space law does not satisfy it unless
a Borel $B$-valued realization is separately constructed.

and hence

A topological space $X$ is **second countable** when its topology has a basis $\mathcal B$ that is at most countable (Basis and subbasis for a topology, and the topology generated by a family of sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). $$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library

$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.
