The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be a nonempty oriented smooth link with $r\ge1$ components, and let $X_L=S^3\setminus L$ be its open complement. For each component choose a smooth fibrewise norm on its normal plane bundle $\nu(K_i)$ and a tubular map $\Phi_i$ from an open neighborhood of the zero section, fixing the zero section, together with a radius $\epsilon_i>0$ whose closed disk subbundle lies in that neighborhood. Require the resulting closed tubes $N(K_i)=\Phi_i(D_{\epsilon_i}\nu(K_i))$ to be pairwise disjoint, and put $N(L)=\bigcup_{i=1}^rN(K_i)$ and $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(L)$, the resulting compact smooth $3$-manifold with boundary. The tube choices are part of the input. Choose a basepoint $b\in E_L\subset X_L$. Orient each normal disk so that the positive tangent to $K_i$ followed by its positive normal basis agrees with the fixed orientation of $S^3$. A **positive meridian** $\mu_i$ of $K_i$ is the oriented boundary of the radius-$\epsilon_i$ normal disk in one fibre of $\nu(K_i)$; the curve lies on $\partial E_L$ and is disjoint from every component of $L$; its spanning normal disk meets $K_i$ transversely once with positive sign and misses every other component. Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^r$ and identifies the classes of $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r$ with its standard basis. Write $G=\pi_1(X_L,b)$ and let $\phi:G\to H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ be the first Hurewicz homomorphism, equivalently abelianization. The subgroup $\ker\phi$ is normal. The connected covering $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$ classified by $\ker\phi$ is the **maximal abelian cover**; it is regular and its deck group is identified with $G/\ker\phi\cong H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$. Put $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)]\cong\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$, where $t_i$ is the deck transformation corresponding to $[\mu_i]$. The isomorphism sends each variable to its group-ring basis element; monomials $t_1^{n_1}\cdots t_r^{n_r}$ correspond bijectively to the basis elements indexed by $n_1[\mu_1]+\cdots+n_r[\mu_r]$. Define the absolute multivariable Alexander module by

$$A_L=H_1(X_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z),$$

as a left $\Lambda_r$-module under the deck action. “Absolute” means this is ordinary homology of the covering space, not relative homology with respect to a fibre over the basepoint.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

Let $B$ be nonempty, path-connected, locally path-connected, and semilocally simply connected, fix $b_0\in B$, and put $G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$.

1. The assignment $$[p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)]\longmapsto p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$$ is a bijection from based-isomorphism classes of based connected coverings of $B$ to subgroups of $G$.
2. After forgetting the chosen point in the fibre, the assignment to the conjugacy class of $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$ is a bijection from isomorphism classes of connected coverings of $B$ to conjugacy classes of subgroups of $G$.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

For every integer $r\ge1$, the commutative ring
$$
\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]
$$
is Noetherian and a unique factorisation domain. Its units are exactly the elements $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$ with $k_i\in\mathbb Z$.

Let $A\subseteq X$, let $i:A\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion, and choose $a\in A$. If $A$ is a retract of $X$ ([[def-retraction-and-deformation-retract]]), then

$$i_*:\pi_1(A,a)\longrightarrow\pi_1(X,a)$$

is injective. If $A$ is a deformation retract of $X$, the inclusion and retraction induce mutually inverse fundamental-group isomorphisms at every basepoint of $A$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $L$ be a nonempty oriented $r$-component link with $r\ge1$ and maximal-abelian-cover module $A_L$ over $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$. Then $A_L$ is finitely presented, every elementary/Fitting ideal $E_j(A_L)$ is independent of the chosen finite triangulation and of the chosen lifts of its cells, and the order $\operatorname{ord}(A_L)$—the greatest common divisor of the generators of $E_q(A_L)$, where $q=\dim_{\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r)}(A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r}\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r))$—is defined up to a unit $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$. The diagonal ring map $\eta:\Lambda_r\to\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, $t_i\mapsto t$, specializes the lifted chain complex by coefficient extension to the total-linking cyclic-cover chain complex. This statement concerns the chain complex only; it does not identify $A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r,\eta}\Lambda_1$ with the first homology of the specialized complex. For $r\ge2$, the diagonal map is nonflat and such an identification need not hold because homology need not commute with nonflat base change.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the data in the definition of the maximal-abelian-cover Alexander module for a nonempty oriented smooth link $L$. Let $i:E_L\hookrightarrow X_L$ be the inclusion of the compact exterior into the open complement, and let $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$ be the maximal abelian cover. Then $E_L$ is a strong deformation retract of $X_L$, the restricted covering $p^{-1}(E_L)\to E_L$ is the connected maximal abelian cover of $E_L$, and the lifted deformation retract is equivariant under the deck group. The inclusion identifies $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ and preserves the positive-meridian classes. In particular, inclusion induces a $\Lambda_r$-module isomorphism

$$
H_1(p^{-1}(E_L);\mathbb Z)\cong A_L.
$$
Let $p:E\to B$ be a covering, $H:Y\times I\to B$ a homotopy, and $\widetilde H_0:Y\to E$ a lift of $H(-,0)$. There is a unique lift $\widetilde H:Y\times I\to E$ of $H$ extending $\widetilde H_0$.

Let $A\subseteq X$, let $i:A\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion, and choose $a\in A$. If $A$ is a retract of $X$ ([[def-retraction-and-deformation-retract]]), then

$$i_*:\pi_1(A,a)\longrightarrow\pi_1(X,a)$$

is injective. If $A$ is a deformation retract of $X$, the inclusion and retraction induce mutually inverse fundamental-group isomorphisms at every basepoint of $A$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as in the maximal-abelian-cover convention. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be a nonempty oriented smooth link, with $r\ge1$, compact exterior $E_L$ formed by deleting the interiors of pairwise-disjoint chosen closed normal-disk tubes, and basepoint $b\in E_L$. For a knot, $r=1$ and $E_L=E_K$. The full meridian abelianization group is $H_L=H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$, with the positive normal-disk meridians as its ordered basis. Choose a finite-rank free abelian group $H$ of positive rank and an epimorphism $\chi:H_L\to H$; write $\psi=\chi\circ\mathrm{ab}:G\to H$ for the induced map from $G=\pi_1(E_L,b)$. The identity choice $H=H_L$ is the full multivariable deck map; a coloring may identify its variables only through the explicitly stated map $\chi$. Let $\mathbb F$ be a field, let $d\ge1$, and let $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$ be a representation. Put $\Lambda=\mathbb F[H]$, the commutative Laurent-polynomial ring with monomial basis $H$, and $Q=\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda)$. On row vectors define the right $\mathbb F[G]$ action by $v\cdot g=v\rho(g)\psi(g)$, where $\psi(g)$ is central multiplication by its monomial in $\Lambda$. For a chosen finite based CW structure $X$ on $E_L$, orient and order its cells and choose one lift of each cell to the universal cover $\widetilde X$. The twisted cellular complex is

$$C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\Lambda^d)=\Lambda^d\otimes_{\mathbb F[G]}C_*(\widetilde X;\mathbb F),$$

and its fraction-field complex is $C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;Q^d)=Q\otimes_{\Lambda}C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\Lambda^d)$. The lifted cell bases and the standard coordinate basis of $\mathbb F^d$ give the based $Q$-vector-space bases. If this fraction-field complex is not acyclic, define its twisted torsion to be $0$. If it is acyclic, choose in each degree a basis $\mathbf b_i$ of $B_i=\operatorname{im}\partial_{i+1}$ and lifts $\widetilde{\mathbf b}_{i-1}$ of $\mathbf b_{i-1}$ under $\partial_i$; with $\mathbf c_i$ the based cellular basis, set

$$\tau(C_*,\mathbf c)=\prod_i[\mathbf b_i,\widetilde{\mathbf b}_{i-1}/\mathbf c_i]^{(-1)^{i+1}}\in Q^\times,$$

where brackets denote the determinant of the change-of-basis matrix. The twisted Reidemeister torsion is this value modulo the subgroup $\mathcal U_{\rho,\psi}=\{\pm\det(\rho(g))\psi(g)^d:g\in G\}\subset Q^\times$. This exact determinant image is contained in the commonly used coarser unit subgroup $\{\pm a h:a\in\det(\rho(G)),\ h\in H\}$. The choice-free statement uses the full abelianization chain model first and specializes it only by the declared coefficient map $\chi$.

Let $X$ be a certified based deficiency-one exterior spine with one $0$-cell, $n\ge2$ $1$-cells and $n-1$ $2$-cells, let $\psi:\pi_1(X)\twoheadrightarrow H\cong\mathbb Z^m$ have $m\ge1$, let $\rho:\pi_1(X)\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$, and let $H_1(C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\mathbb F[H]^d))$ be torsion over $\mathbb F[H]$. Form the Fox block matrix $J$ and a chosen Wada column quotient $W_j=\det(J_{\widehat j})/D_j$ with $D_j=\det(\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)-I_d)\ne0$. Then the fraction-field complex is acyclic, $\det(J_{\widehat j})\ne0$, and $W_j$ equals its based twisted Reidemeister torsion in $Q^\times/\mathcal U_{\rho,\psi}$. Every admissible deleted column gives the same class. This conclusion applies only to the specified cellular spine; an abstract presentation of the same group is insufficient.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $\beta=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a geometric braid with
the fixed real basepoints $q_j=((2j-n-1)/(4(n+1)),0)$ and endpoint
permutation $\pi$, as in [[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]].
Identify the disk with $\{x\in\mathbb C:|x|<1\}$ and put
$$V=(D^\circ\times[0,1])/((x,1)\sim(x,0)).$$
The quotient and its topology use [[def-product-topology]] and the circle
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of [[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]].
The interval images
$$s_j=\{[(z_j(t),t)]:0\le t\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\beta)=\bigcup_{j=1}^n s_j$$
are the **closure in the open solid torus**. In general an individual
$s_j$ is an interval image, not a closed circle: its last point is the
first point of $s_{\pi(j)}$.

**Components and orientation.** For a cycle
$(j,\pi(j),\ldots,\pi^{k-1}(j))$ concatenate these $k$ strand maps in
that order, with parameter in $[0,k]$. Their endpoints agree in $V$,
so the concatenation factors through $\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$.
It is injective on this circle: points at distinct nonintegral heights
can agree only when their parameters have the same fractional part,
and the distinct strands at that height have distinct disk coordinates;
at integral heights only the specified adjacent endpoints agree.
Thus each cycle gives an embedded circle. Different cycles give
disjoint circles, and every strand belongs to exactly one cycle.
These circles are precisely the connected components of the closure.
The orientation is increasing concatenation parameter. In particular
the number of components equals the number of cycles of $\pi$.

**The standard axis and fixed framing.** In
$S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, as in
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], set
$$A=\{(0,w):|w|=1\},\qquad P_\theta=\{(z,w)\in S^3:z\ne0,\ \arg z=\theta\}.$$
Fix the following particular diffeomorphism, including its disk framing:
$$\varphi([(x,t)])=  \bigl(\sqrt{1-|x|^2}\,e^{2\pi it},x\bigr):  V\longrightarrow S^3\setminus A.$$
Its inverse has disk coordinate $x=w$ and circle coordinate
$[t]=[\arg z/(2\pi)]$. Every $P_\theta$ is consequently an open disk.
The **raw topological oriented closure** is
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{top}}=\varphi(\operatorname{cl}(\beta)).$$
This explicit $\varphi$ is part of the construction; the definition
does not allow an arbitrary page-preserving change of framing.

**Page intersections and smooth representatives.** The whole closure
meets every page in exactly $n$ points. A component belonging to a
$\pi$-cycle of length $k$ meets each page in exactly $k$ points:
at any fractional height it uses exactly those $k$ distinct strands.
The page coordinate of its concatenation is $[t]$, for
$t\in\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$, so its oriented degree is $+k$.
If all disk-coordinate strand maps are smooth and have all positive-order derivatives
zero at their endpoints, their cycle concatenations have matching jets
at every seam. The page coordinate has nonzero derivative, so the
result is a smooth embedding of disjoint oriented circles, in the
sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. For an endpoint-flat smooth braid, its literal $\varphi$-image is therefore a smooth oriented link and is denoted $\widehat\beta$.

**Closure in the smooth oriented-link category.** The raw image need not be smooth, even if individual strands are smooth but their endpoint jets fail to match at the cycle seams. For an arbitrary continuous braid, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) and choose a smooth representative $\beta_s$ by [[lem-every-geometric-braid-is-braid-isotopic-to-a-smooth-braid]]. Make it endpoint-flat by composing all disk-coordinate strands with a fixed smooth nondecreasing $\psi:I\to I$, equal to $0$ near $0$ and $1$ near $1$. Interpolation of height maps $(1-u)t+u\psi(t)$ is an endpoint-fixed braid isotopy, because every strand is evaluated at the same height. The smooth-category closure of $\beta$ is the oriented-link isotopy class of this chosen model's literal $\varphi$-image; when a subset is needed, use that chosen closed-braid representative. Independence of the representative is proved by [[lem-closure-depends-only-on-the-braid-isotopy-class]]. Page and cycle properties refer to the chosen constructed closed braid, with the same number of strands and endpoint permutation as $\beta$.

If $\beta$ already has smooth strands with matching cycle-seam jets, in particular if it is endpoint-flat, its literal raw image is a smooth link and is retained as $\widehat\beta$. The raw quotient, fixed $\varphi$, finite cycles, page counts and trivial closures remain choice-free. Finite elementary words have explicit smooth endpoint-flat models, so forming their literal closures also requires no choice assumption; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used for the general continuous-representative convention and its independence theorem.

**The trivial closure.** For the constant braid its circles are
$\{(\sqrt{1-q_j^2}e^{2\pi it},q_j):[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\}$.
They are latitudes of the sphere
$S=\{(z,w)\in S^3:\operatorname{Im}w=0\}$, with
$\operatorname{Re}w=q_j$. Each northern cap
$C_j=\{p\in S:\operatorname{Re}w(p)\ge q_j\}$ is a smooth disk:
stereographic coordinates on $S$ give radius
$\sqrt{(1-q_j)/(1+q_j)}$ for this cap. To make their spanning disks
disjoint, let $e$ be the unit vector in the $\operatorname{Im}w$
direction, set $\varepsilon=\pi/16$ and
$f_j(p)=\varepsilon(\operatorname{Re}w(p)-q_j)$ on $C_j$, and use
$$F_j(p)=\cos(f_j(p))p+\sin(f_j(p))e.$$
The boundary is fixed. The tubular parametrization
$(p,s)\mapsto\cos(s)p+\sin(s)e$ is injective for $|s|<\pi/2$,
and $0\le f_j<\pi/8$. On overlapping caps, if $q_i<q_j$ then
$f_i-f_j=\varepsilon(q_j-q_i)>0$, so their graphs are disjoint.
Thus these are pairwise disjoint smooth spanning disks. The trivial
$n$-braid closes to the oriented $n$-component unlink; for $n=1$
this is the unknot.

At $n=0$ all strand and cycle unions are empty, every page has zero intersections,
and the closure is the empty link. The basepoint list and disk constructions
above then have no entries.

Let $F_n=\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle$ be the free group of
[[def-free-group]], identified with $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$ through the
standard meridians by
[[thm-the-punctured-disk-fundamental-group-is-free-on-standard-meridians]]. For
$1\le i\le n-1$, $\rho(\sigma_i)\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ is the automorphism
given on the basis by
$$\rho(\sigma_i)(x_i)=x_ix_{i+1}x_i^{-1},\qquad \rho(\sigma_i)(x_{i+1})=x_i, \qquad \rho(\sigma_i)(x_j)=x_j\ (j\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$
Its inverse is
$$\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_i)=x_{i+1},\qquad \rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_{i+1})=x_{i+1}^{-1}x_ix_{i+1},\qquad \rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_j)=x_j\ (j\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$
Products use ordinary function composition: the leftmost factor is the
outermost map and the rightmost factor acts first. Also
$\rho(\sigma_i^{-1}):=\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}$.

**The assignments are automorphisms, and the displayed formulas are inverse.**
By the universal property of the free group
([[def-free-group]], [[thm-reduced-words-form-the-free-group]]) the displayed
values on the free basis extend to a unique endomorphism
$\rho(\sigma_i):F_n\to F_n$, and likewise the displayed inverse formulas extend
to an endomorphism $\theta:F_n\to F_n$. Substituting,
$$\theta\bigl(\rho(\sigma_i)(x_i)\bigr)=\theta(x_ix_{i+1}x_i^{-1}) =\theta(x_i)\,\theta(x_{i+1})\,\theta(x_i)^{-1} =x_{i+1}\,\bigl(x_{i+1}^{-1}x_ix_{i+1}\bigr)\,x_{i+1}^{-1}=x_i,$$
$$\theta\bigl(\rho(\sigma_i)(x_{i+1})\bigr)=\theta(x_i)=x_{i+1},$$
and both composites fix every other basis element; so
$\theta\circ\rho(\sigma_i)=\operatorname{id}_{F_n}$ on a basis, hence as
endomorphisms. Symmetrically $\rho(\sigma_i)\circ\theta=
\operatorname{id}_{F_n}$. Therefore $\rho(\sigma_i)$ is a bijection with the
displayed inverse, i.e. an automorphism
([[def-group-isomorphism-and-automorphism]]).

**Convention note.** The displayed formulas are Artin's equations (14) and (15)
with the letter $\sigma_i$ and its inverse interchanged; under the frozen
geometric conventions of this library the *positive* half twist is the
anticlockwise supported half rotation (see
`def-elementary-geometric-half-twist` and
`thm-braid-group-is-the-boundary-fixed-mapping-class-group-of-the-punctured-disk`),
and
`prop-the-geometric-action-on-meridians-is-the-artin-representation` proves
that its action on the standard meridians is exactly the substitution frozen
above. The interchange is a convention, not a change of mathematical content:
$\rho$ and Artin's substitution generate the same subgroup of
$\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ and satisfy the same braid relations, and the
companion page shows that the mirror (clockwise) half rotation realizes
Artin's displayed formulas verbatim.

By [[lem-artin-automorphisms-satisfy-the-braid-relations]] the assignment
$\sigma_i\mapsto\rho(\sigma_i)$ satisfies the defining relations of the
presented braid group $B_n$ of
[[def-braid-group-by-the-artin-presentation]], so von Dyck's theorem
[[thm-von-dyck]] yields a unique homomorphism
$$\rho:B_n\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(F_n).$$
This is the **Artin representation**; it is the frozen convention for every
later statement of the page.

**Uniqueness and effectivity.** The homomorphism is unique because it is
prescribed on the generating set $\{\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}\}$, and it is
computed on a braid word by composing the finitely many automorphisms
$\rho(\sigma_i)^{\pm1}$ attached to its letters, as frozen in
[[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]]. No choice principle and no
geometric input are used in the construction; von Dyck's theorem
[[thm-von-dyck]] supplies existence and uniqueness of the extension.

Assume AC. Let $G_n$ be the geometric braid group,
$\varphi_n:B_n\to G_n$ the published surjection of
[[prop-the-artin-presentation-surjects-onto-geometric-braids]], and
$$\Psi:G_n\longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}(D^2,Q_n;\partial D^2)$$
the isomorphism of
[[thm-braid-group-is-the-boundary-fixed-mapping-class-group-of-the-punctured-disk]].
Identifying $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$ with $F_n$ by the standard meridians of
[[def-standard-meridians-of-a-punctured-disk]], the automorphism of $F_n$
induced by the mapping class $\Psi(\varphi_n(\beta))$ equals $\rho(\beta)$ for
every braid word $\beta$. In particular the geometric half twist $\sigma_i$ acts
as the Nielsen automorphism of
[[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]].

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $D^2=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|\le1\}$ and
$Q_n=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the closed unit disk and the base configuration of
[[def-boundary-fixed-mapping-class-group-of-a-punctured-disk]], so that
$q_1<\dots<q_n$ are distinct points of the real axis of
$\operatorname{int}D^2$. Fix the boundary basepoint
$$d:=(0,1)\in\partial D^2 .$$
For $1\le i\le n$ let $s_i\colon[0,1]\to D^2$ be the **straight stem**
$$s_i(t):=(1-t)\,d+t\,q_i ,$$
the straight segment from $d$ to $q_i$, and choose a round circle $C_i$ in
$D^2\setminus Q_n$ centred at $q_i$, of radius $0<\varepsilon_i<d(q_i,\partial D^2)$
so small that the closed disks $B_i$ bounded by the circles are pairwise disjoint, that each circle meets only its own stem, and that it meets $s_i$ exactly once, at
$p_i:=s_i(1-\varepsilon_i/L_i)$ where $L_i:=|d-q_i|$, and meets no other stem
$s_j$ with $j\ne i$. Write $c_i\colon[0,1]\to D^2\setminus Q_n$ for $C_i$
traversed once **positively** (counterclockwise), from $p_i$ back to $p_i$.
The **standard meridian loops** are the loops based at $d$
$$x_i:=s_i\,c_i\,s_i^{-1},\qquad 1\le i\le n,$$
read as $s_i$ from $d$ to $p_i$, then $c_i$, then $s_i$ from $p_i$ back to $d$
([[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]]). Further, $\partial$ denotes the
**positively oriented boundary loop**
$$\partial(t):=d\,e^{2\pi i t},\qquad t\in[0,1],$$
of $D^2$ based at $d$: it traverses $\partial D^2$ once counterclockwise,
starting and ending at $d$.

**Existence and independence of the choices.** The straight segments $s_i$
leave $d$ in pairwise distinct directions (the points $q_1,\dots,q_n$ are
distinct and lie strictly below $d$) and meet one another only at $d$; the
segments $s_i$ meet the real axis only at their endpoints $q_i$. An explicit choice-free family is given by
$$\varepsilon_i=\frac14\min\left(\{1-|q_i|\}\cup\left\{|q_i-q_j|,\frac{|q_i-q_j|}{\sqrt{1+q_j^2}}:j\ne i\right\}\right).$$
The finite set inside the minimum is nonempty and contains only positive
numbers. The distance from $q_i$ to the line through $d,q_j$ is
$|q_i-q_j|/\sqrt{1+q_j^2}$, so $B_i$ misses every other stem. Also
$\varepsilon_i+\varepsilon_j\le|q_i-q_j|/2<|q_i-q_j|$, proving disjointness
of the **closed** disks, and $\varepsilon_i<1-|q_i|$ keeps each disk inside
$D^2$. The radius is less than $|d-q_i|$, giving exactly the displayed contact
with its own stem. For $n=1$ the minimum has only its boundary-margin entry;
for $n=0$ the family is empty. Any family satisfying these conditions may be
fixed; this formula witnesses its existence without any choice axiom.

The class $[x_i]\in\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$ is independent of
all admissible radii, including the old broader convention requiring only
avoidance of the other stems. Such a circle encloses no $q_j$ with $j\ne i$:
otherwise the other stem from $d$, which lies outside the circle, to $q_j$
would cross it (or have $q_j$ on it). Thus the larger disk of any two admissible
concentric circles still contains no other puncture. Interpolate their radii
and their tether contact points radially; this is a based lasso homotopy in
$D^2\setminus Q_n$ ([[def-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy]]).
It does not require the intermediate circle to be disjoint from the other
circles, so the class argument does not circularly assume the newly explicit
representative convention. Fix once and
for all one such family of circles; every statement on this page uses that
fixed family.

**Frozen conventions of the page.** The stems and the basepoint transport are
fixed once and for all by the choices above; the stems are indexed so that the
positively oriented boundary loop $\partial$, as seen from $d$, meets the
directions of the stems in the order $s_1,s_2,\dots,s_n$. Products of braid
automorphisms use ordinary function composition: the leftmost factor is the
outermost map, so the rightmost factor acts first. No relation of the braid presentation and no choice principle
is used in this definition.

Let $F_n=\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle$ be the free group of
[[def-free-group]] on $n$ letters. The assignment $x_i\mapsto[x_i]$ extends to
a group isomorphism $F_n\to\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$; equivalently, the
classes $[x_1],\dots,[x_n]$ of the standard meridians of
[[def-standard-meridians-of-a-punctured-disk]] form a free basis of
$\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$.

Let $X$ be the based presentation $2$-complex with one vertex, oriented $1$-cells $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, and oriented $2$-cells attached along words $r_1,\ldots,r_m$ in the free group $F_n$. Let $G=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$ be its presented fundamental group, let $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$ be a representation, and let $\psi:G\to H$ be the declared free-abelian deck map. For $\Phi:\mathbb F[F_n]\to M_d(Q)$ induced by $x_j\mapsto\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)$, the twisted differential $\partial_1$ has blocks $\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)-I_d$, and the $i$th block row of $\partial_2$ is

$$\left(\Phi\left(\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial x_1}\right),\ldots,\Phi\left(\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial x_n}\right)\right),$$

where coefficient vectors are written as rows and differentials act on the right: the matrix of $\partial_1$ is the stacked column of blocks $\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)-I_d$, while the matrix of $\partial_2$ is the $md$-by-$nd$ block matrix whose $i$th row is the displayed Fox row. The Fox derivatives use the product and inverse recursions in the Wada definition. Thus the evaluated Fox-Jacobian blocks are exactly the cellular boundary blocks of the based twisted complex of this presentation $2$-complex.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L$ be a nonempty oriented smooth $r$-component link with $r\ge1$, compact exterior $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(L)$ obtained from pairwise-disjoint closed normal disk tubes, a finite oriented simplicial triangulation $K$ of $E_L$ with ordered vertices and simplices, with least vertex $v_0$ as the basepoint used in the cover definition, and one certified positive-meridian edge loop $\mu_i$ per component. Orient each normal disk so the positive tangent to its component followed by the positive disk basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$, and assume the resulting classes form the standard basis of $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$. If an integer-vector edge labeling is antisymmetric under edge reversal, sums to zero on every oriented 2-simplex, and evaluates to the $i$th standard basis vector on $\mu_i$, then the chain procedure returns a finite free chain complex over $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$. The first homology of this complex is the absolute maximal-abelian-cover Alexander module $A_L$. Its Fitting ideals are independent of the triangulation and cell lifts, and its order is defined up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

If $D$ is an integral domain, then $D\setminus\{0\}$ is multiplicative. Its localisation
$$ \operatorname{Frac}(D)=(D\setminus\{0\})^{-1}D $$
is the **field of fractions** of $D$. Thus its elements are fractions $a/b$ with $a,b\in D$ and $b\ne0$, modulo the localisation equivalence relation.

For every integral domain $D$, the localisation $\operatorname{Frac}(D)$ is a field. Its canonical map
$$ D\longrightarrow\operatorname{Frac}(D),\qquad d\longmapsto d/1, $$
is an injective unital ring homomorphism.

derivations.claim: Let $\alpha(g)=\rho(g)\psi(g)$ denote the coefficient matrix. Under [A1], the supplied filling certificate and [F7] identify $\pi_1(X)$ as the quotient of $\pi_1(Y)$ that kills the axis meridian $x$. Pulling the coefficient system back from $X$ therefore gives $\alpha(x)=I_d$ and $\psi(x)=1$; the core of $V$ is represented on $T$ by $g_n$, with matrix $M_n$. The algorithm forms the full positive-meridian basis on $X$ before applying $\chi$, while the compatible filling certificate specifies the resulting pulled-back or extended coefficient systems on $Y,T,V$ and makes them agree on overlaps. The chain-model theorem [F6] supplies the maximal-abelian-cover module computation on the full system; it does not prescribe the specialization order. The map $\pi_1(Y)\to\pi_1(X)$ is surjective, so the pulled-back deck map on $Y$ is still onto and the coefficient-unit images for the two exteriors agree. Since $D\ne0$, $M_n-I_d$ is invertible.

First compute the core-circle spine $V_{\mathrm{core}}$ with one $0$-cell and one $1$-cell for $g_n$. Its twisted boundary is $M_n-I_d$, so this core complex is acyclic and its torsion is $D^{-1}$. This core is not used as a CW pair containing $T$; a separate relative model and its torsion comparison are established before applying the gluing sequence. Give $T$ the standard one-vertex CW structure with $1$-cells $x,g_n$ and one commutator $2$-cell $xg_nx^{-1}g_n^{-1}$. The Fox boundary blocks are $d_1=(0,M_n-I_d)^\mathsf{T}$ and $d_2=(I_d-M_n,0)$: hence $d_1$ is onto, $d_2$ is injective onto $\ker d_1$, and $T$ is acyclic. In the torsion determinant product, the factors $\det(I_d-M_n)$ and $\det((M_n-I_d)^{-1})$ cancel up to $(-1)^d$, so $\tau(T)=(-1)^d$.

Give $D^2$ its boundary vertex, boundary edge $x$, and meridian disk cell $a$, and give $S^1$ its vertex and core edge $g_n$. Their product is a finite CW model $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ of the actual solid torus containing exactly the specified torus CW structure as its boundary subcomplex. Besides the cells of $T$, it has the $2$-cell $a\times\{*\}$, still denoted $a$, and the $3$-cell $b=a\times g_n$. Put $A=M_n-I_d$ and let $q$ denote the torus $2$-cell, with the orientation in step 2.1. For a coefficient row $v$, the product boundaries are
$$\partial a(v)=x(v),\qquad \partial q(v)=x(-vA),\qquad \partial b(v)=q(v)+a(vA).$$
The first formula is the meridian disk boundary, the second is the torus Fox boundary from step 2.1, and the third is the oriented boundary of disk times core edge; its two terms have cancelling images under $\partial$. Replace the degree-two block $q(v)$ by $q'(v)=q(v)+a(vA)$. This block-triangular basis change has determinant one, $\partial q'=0$, and $\partial b(v)=q'(v)$. Split off the unit two-term pair $(b,q')$, then the unit pair $(a,x)$. The remaining based complex is exactly the core complex with $\partial g_n(v)=vA$. Each split pair has identity incidence and torsion one up to the sign unit, and the triangular change contributes determinant one. Hence $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ has the same homology and torsion class as $V_{\mathrm{core}}$, so it is acyclic and its torsion is $D^{-1}$ up to the declared units. This calculation supplies the missing based comparison while retaining $T$ in the actual gluing model.

For $X$, Fox differentiation of $r_i=g_i^{-1}\beta_*(g_i)$ gives block row $M_i^{-1}(\widetilde B_{i,*}-e_i)$, where $e_i$ is the $i$th identity block row and $M_i=\rho(g_i)\psi(g_i)$. Thus, after deleting the $g_n$ column, the Fox block is $\operatorname{diag}(M_1^{-1},\ldots,M_{n-1}^{-1})(\overline B_\rho(\beta)-I)$, whose determinant is $\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\det(M_i^{-1})\right)N$. The prefactor is a nonzero coefficient unit. The $d_1$ block for $g_n$ is $M_n-I_d$, which is invertible, so $d_1$ is onto and projection from $\ker d_1$ to the first $n-1$ coordinate blocks is an isomorphism. By [F5], the projected $d_2$ is the displayed deleted Fox block. Therefore $N\ne0$ implies $d_2$ injective and, by dimensions and $d_1d_2=0$, the complex is acyclic; if the complex is acyclic, the same projection makes $d_2$ injective and forces $N\ne0$. Hence nonacyclicity is equivalent to $N=0$.

Use the relative-cellular gluing operation [F9] for the actual decomposition in the supplied certificate. For $V$ use $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ from step 2.2, not its core spine. For the exterior pieces the operation uses the compatible relative CW representatives and the supplied based simple-spine comparisons. Equivalently, a boundary map into a spine is represented by its finite cellular mapping cylinder: each added prism over a torus cell pairs with its source face, with lifted incidence a unit; these pairs are removed in decreasing cell dimension. Their torsion changes lie in the declared unit subgroup. Thus the based torsion classes used below are those of the supplied spines, without identifying the boundary torus with a subcomplex of a core circle or of an abstract presentation. In the common relative models each cell of $T$ occurs in both pieces, and each other cell occurs in exactly one. Inclusion into the first piece and its negative into the second, followed by the difference quotient to the union, therefore give the degreewise split short exact sequence
$$0\longrightarrow C_*(T)\longrightarrow C_*(Y_{\mathrm{rel}})\oplus C_*(V_{\mathrm{rel}})\longrightarrow C_*(X_{\mathrm{rel}})\longrightarrow0.$$
Choose the shared lifts compatibly; any permitted adjustment changes only the declared determinant/deck units. Since $T$ and $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ are acyclic by steps 2.1 and 2.2, the long exact homology sequence identifies $H_*(Y;Q^d)$ with $H_*(X;Q^d)$. Thus $Y$ is acyclic exactly when $X$ is. Subsequent references to the gluing sequence mean these relative models and their certified based comparisons.

In the acyclic case, choose boundary bases in the short exact sequence compatibly: lift a basis of each quotient boundary space, append a basis of the subcomplex boundary space, and lift the resulting boundary bases to chain groups. The change-of-basis matrices are block triangular with diagonal blocks the matrices for the subcomplex and quotient, so their determinants multiply degree by degree; the alternating torsion product therefore gives $\tau(Y)\tau(V)=\pm\tau(T)\tau(X)$. As $\tau(T)=\pm1$ and both signs lie in the declared unit subgroup, step 2.1 yields $\tau(Y)\doteq\tau(X)D$.

Suppose $X$ and hence $Y$ are acyclic over $Q$. The finite based chain modules over $\Lambda=\mathbb F[H]$ are free. If $z\in C_1(Y;\Lambda^d)$ is a $1$-cycle, acyclicity over $Q$ gives $z/1=d_2(y)/s$ for some $y\in C_2(Y;\Lambda^d)$ and nonzero $s\in\Lambda$. By [F8], equality in the fraction field means that some nonzero $u\in\Lambda$ annihilates $sz-d_2(y)$; since $C_1(Y;\Lambda^d)$ is free over the domain $\Lambda$, multiplication by $u$ is injective, so $sz=d_2(y)$. Every degree-one homology class is therefore killed by a nonzero element of $\Lambda$.

Apply [F2] to the certified spine of $Y$ and delete the $g_n$ column, whose denominator is $D\ne0$. For $s_i=\beta_*(g_i)(x^{-1}g_ix)^{-1}$, the $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ Fox blocks evaluate to $\widetilde B-I$, where $\widetilde B$ is the full cumulative-meridian Fox matrix, and the $x$-column blocks are $I_d-M_i$ with $M_i=\rho(g_i)\psi(g_i)$. Because $\beta_*(g_n)=g_n$, the last row of $\widetilde B-I$ is zero; after deleting its $g_n$ column, the remaining matrix has upper-left block $\overline B_\rho(\beta)-I$, arbitrary upper-right block, zero lower-left block, and lower-right block $I_d-M_n$. It is block upper triangular, so its determinant is $(-1)^dND$. Dividing by $D$ gives $(-1)^dN$, which represents $N$ modulo the sign unit. Consequently $\tau(Y)\doteq N$.

If the complex is acyclic, combine steps 4.1 and 5.1 to obtain $\tau(X)D\doteq N$, hence $\tau(X)\doteq N/D$. If it is nonacyclic, step 2.3 gives $N=0$, and the declared convention sets $\tau(X)=0=N/D$. This proves the statement in both branches.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as in the maximal-abelian-cover convention. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be a nonempty oriented smooth link, with $r\ge1$, compact exterior $E_L$ formed by deleting the interiors of pairwise-disjoint chosen closed normal-disk tubes, and basepoint $b\in E_L$. For a knot, $r=1$ and $E_L=E_K$. The full meridian abelianization group is $H_L=H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$, with the positive normal-disk meridians as its ordered basis. Choose a finite-rank free abelian group $H$ of positive rank and an epimorphism $\chi:H_L\to H$; write $\psi=\chi\circ\mathrm{ab}:G\to H$ for the induced map from $G=\pi_1(E_L,b)$. The identity choice $H=H_L$ is the full multivariable deck map; a coloring may identify its variables only through the explicitly stated map $\chi$. Let $\mathbb F$ be a field, let $d\ge1$, and let $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$ be a representation. Put $\Lambda=\mathbb F[H]$, the commutative Laurent-polynomial ring with monomial basis $H$, and $Q=\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda)$. On row vectors define the right $\mathbb F[G]$ action by $v\cdot g=v\rho(g)\psi(g)$, where $\psi(g)$ is central multiplication by its monomial in $\Lambda$. For a chosen finite based CW structure $X$ on $E_L$, orient and order its cells and choose one lift of each cell to the universal cover $\widetilde X$. The twisted cellular complex is

$$C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\Lambda^d)=\Lambda^d\otimes_{\mathbb F[G]}C_*(\widetilde X;\mathbb F),$$

and its fraction-field complex is $C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;Q^d)=Q\otimes_{\Lambda}C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\Lambda^d)$. The lifted cell bases and the standard coordinate basis of $\mathbb F^d$ give the based $Q$-vector-space bases. If this fraction-field complex is not acyclic, define its twisted torsion to be $0$. If it is acyclic, choose in each degree a basis $\mathbf b_i$ of $B_i=\operatorname{im}\partial_{i+1}$ and lifts $\widetilde{\mathbf b}_{i-1}$ of $\mathbf b_{i-1}$ under $\partial_i$; with $\mathbf c_i$ the based cellular basis, set

$$\tau(C_*,\mathbf c)=\prod_i[\mathbf b_i,\widetilde{\mathbf b}_{i-1}/\mathbf c_i]^{(-1)^{i+1}}\in Q^\times,$$

where brackets denote the determinant of the change-of-basis matrix. The twisted Reidemeister torsion is this value modulo the subgroup $\mathcal U_{\rho,\psi}=\{\pm\det(\rho(g))\psi(g)^d:g\in G\}\subset Q^\times$. This exact determinant image is contained in the commonly used coarser unit subgroup $\{\pm a h:a\in\det(\rho(G)),\ h\in H\}$. The choice-free statement uses the full abelianization chain model first and specializes it only by the declared coefficient map $\chi$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as in the maximal-abelian-cover convention. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be a nonempty oriented smooth link, with $r\ge1$, compact exterior $E_L$ formed by deleting the interiors of pairwise-disjoint chosen closed normal-disk tubes, and basepoint $b\in E_L$. For a knot, $r=1$ and $E_L=E_K$. The full meridian abelianization group is $H_L=H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$, with the positive normal-disk meridians as its ordered basis. Choose a finite-rank free abelian group $H$ of positive rank and an epimorphism $\chi:H_L\to H$; write $\psi=\chi\circ\mathrm{ab}:G\to H$ for the induced map from $G=\pi_1(E_L,b)$. The identity choice $H=H_L$ is the full multivariable deck map; a coloring may identify its variables only through the explicitly stated map $\chi$. Let $\mathbb F$ be a field, let $d\ge1$, and let $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$ be a representation. Put $\Lambda=\mathbb F[H]$, the commutative Laurent-polynomial ring with monomial basis $H$, and $Q=\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda)$. On row vectors define the right $\mathbb F[G]$ action by $v\cdot g=v\rho(g)\psi(g)$, where $\psi(g)$ is central multiplication by its monomial in $\Lambda$. For a chosen finite based CW structure $X$ on $E_L$, orient and order its cells and choose one lift of each cell to the universal cover $\widetilde X$. The twisted cellular complex is

$$C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\Lambda^d)=\Lambda^d\otimes_{\mathbb F[G]}C_*(\widetilde X;\mathbb F),$$

and its fraction-field complex is $C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;Q^d)=Q\otimes_{\Lambda}C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\Lambda^d)$. The lifted cell bases and the standard coordinate basis of $\mathbb F^d$ give the based $Q$-vector-space bases. If this fraction-field complex is not acyclic, define its twisted torsion to be $0$. If it is acyclic, choose in each degree a basis $\mathbf b_i$ of $B_i=\operatorname{im}\partial_{i+1}$ and lifts $\widetilde{\mathbf b}_{i-1}$ of $\mathbf b_{i-1}$ under $\partial_i$; with $\mathbf c_i$ the based cellular basis, set

$$\tau(C_*,\mathbf c)=\prod_i[\mathbf b_i,\widetilde{\mathbf b}_{i-1}/\mathbf c_i]^{(-1)^{i+1}}\in Q^\times,$$

where brackets denote the determinant of the change-of-basis matrix. The twisted Reidemeister torsion is this value modulo the subgroup $\mathcal U_{\rho,\psi}=\{\pm\det(\rho(g))\psi(g)^d:g\in G\}\subset Q^\times$. This exact determinant image is contained in the commonly used coarser unit subgroup $\{\pm a h:a\in\det(\rho(G)),\ h\in H\}$. The choice-free statement uses the full abelianization chain model first and specializes it only by the declared coefficient map $\chi$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice convention of the twisted-chain definition. Let $X$ be a certified based deficiency-one exterior spine with one $0$-cell, $n\ge2$ $1$-cells and $n-1$ $2$-cells, let $\psi:\pi_1(X)\twoheadrightarrow H\cong\mathbb Z^m$ have $m\ge1$, let $\rho:\pi_1(X)\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$, and let $H_1(C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\mathbb F[H]^d))$ be torsion over $\mathbb F[H]$. Form the Fox block matrix $J$ and a chosen Wada column quotient $W_j=\det(J_{\widehat j})/D_j$ with $D_j=\det(\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)-I_d)\ne0$. Then the fraction-field complex is acyclic, $\det(J_{\widehat j})\ne0$, and $W_j$ equals its based twisted Reidemeister torsion in $Q^\times/\mathcal U_{\rho,\psi}$. Every admissible deleted column gives the same class. This conclusion applies only to the specified cellular spine; an abstract presentation of the same group is insufficient.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $\beta=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a geometric braid with
the fixed real basepoints $q_j=((2j-n-1)/(4(n+1)),0)$ and endpoint
permutation $\pi$, as in [[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]].
Identify the disk with $\{x\in\mathbb C:|x|<1\}$ and put
$$V=(D^\circ\times[0,1])/((x,1)\sim(x,0)).$$
The quotient and its topology use [[def-product-topology]] and the circle
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of [[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]].
The interval images
$$s_j=\{[(z_j(t),t)]:0\le t\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\beta)=\bigcup_{j=1}^n s_j$$
are the **closure in the open solid torus**. In general an individual
$s_j$ is an interval image, not a closed circle: its last point is the
first point of $s_{\pi(j)}$.

**Components and orientation.** For a cycle
$(j,\pi(j),\ldots,\pi^{k-1}(j))$ concatenate these $k$ strand maps in
that order, with parameter in $[0,k]$. Their endpoints agree in $V$,
so the concatenation factors through $\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$.
It is injective on this circle: points at distinct nonintegral heights
can agree only when their parameters have the same fractional part,
and the distinct strands at that height have distinct disk coordinates;
at integral heights only the specified adjacent endpoints agree.
Thus each cycle gives an embedded circle. Different cycles give
disjoint circles, and every strand belongs to exactly one cycle.
These circles are precisely the connected components of the closure.
The orientation is increasing concatenation parameter. In particular
the number of components equals the number of cycles of $\pi$.

**The standard axis and fixed framing.** In
$S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, as in
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], set
$$A=\{(0,w):|w|=1\},\qquad P_\theta=\{(z,w)\in S^3:z\ne0,\ \arg z=\theta\}.$$
Fix the following particular diffeomorphism, including its disk framing:
$$\varphi([(x,t)])=  \bigl(\sqrt{1-|x|^2}\,e^{2\pi it},x\bigr):  V\longrightarrow S^3\setminus A.$$
Its inverse has disk coordinate $x=w$ and circle coordinate
$[t]=[\arg z/(2\pi)]$. Every $P_\theta$ is consequently an open disk.
The **raw topological oriented closure** is
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{top}}=\varphi(\operatorname{cl}(\beta)).$$
This explicit $\varphi$ is part of the construction; the definition
does not allow an arbitrary page-preserving change of framing.

**Page intersections and smooth representatives.** The whole closure
meets every page in exactly $n$ points. A component belonging to a
$\pi$-cycle of length $k$ meets each page in exactly $k$ points:
at any fractional height it uses exactly those $k$ distinct strands.
The page coordinate of its concatenation is $[t]$, for
$t\in\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$, so its oriented degree is $+k$.
If all disk-coordinate strand maps are smooth and have all positive-order derivatives
zero at their endpoints, their cycle concatenations have matching jets
at every seam. The page coordinate has nonzero derivative, so the
result is a smooth embedding of disjoint oriented circles, in the
sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. For an endpoint-flat smooth braid, its literal $\varphi$-image is therefore a smooth oriented link and is denoted $\widehat\beta$.

**Closure in the smooth oriented-link category.** The raw image need not be smooth, even if individual strands are smooth but their endpoint jets fail to match at the cycle seams. For an arbitrary continuous braid, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) and choose a smooth representative $\beta_s$ by [[lem-every-geometric-braid-is-braid-isotopic-to-a-smooth-braid]]. Make it endpoint-flat by composing all disk-coordinate strands with a fixed smooth nondecreasing $\psi:I\to I$, equal to $0$ near $0$ and $1$ near $1$. Interpolation of height maps $(1-u)t+u\psi(t)$ is an endpoint-fixed braid isotopy, because every strand is evaluated at the same height. The smooth-category closure of $\beta$ is the oriented-link isotopy class of this chosen model's literal $\varphi$-image; when a subset is needed, use that chosen closed-braid representative. Independence of the representative is proved by [[lem-closure-depends-only-on-the-braid-isotopy-class]]. Page and cycle properties refer to the chosen constructed closed braid, with the same number of strands and endpoint permutation as $\beta$.

If $\beta$ already has smooth strands with matching cycle-seam jets, in particular if it is endpoint-flat, its literal raw image is a smooth link and is retained as $\widehat\beta$. The raw quotient, fixed $\varphi$, finite cycles, page counts and trivial closures remain choice-free. Finite elementary words have explicit smooth endpoint-flat models, so forming their literal closures also requires no choice assumption; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used for the general continuous-representative convention and its independence theorem.

**The trivial closure.** For the constant braid its circles are
$\{(\sqrt{1-q_j^2}e^{2\pi it},q_j):[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\}$.
They are latitudes of the sphere
$S=\{(z,w)\in S^3:\operatorname{Im}w=0\}$, with
$\operatorname{Re}w=q_j$. Each northern cap
$C_j=\{p\in S:\operatorname{Re}w(p)\ge q_j\}$ is a smooth disk:
stereographic coordinates on $S$ give radius
$\sqrt{(1-q_j)/(1+q_j)}$ for this cap. To make their spanning disks
disjoint, let $e$ be the unit vector in the $\operatorname{Im}w$
direction, set $\varepsilon=\pi/16$ and
$f_j(p)=\varepsilon(\operatorname{Re}w(p)-q_j)$ on $C_j$, and use
$$F_j(p)=\cos(f_j(p))p+\sin(f_j(p))e.$$
The boundary is fixed. The tubular parametrization
$(p,s)\mapsto\cos(s)p+\sin(s)e$ is injective for $|s|<\pi/2$,
and $0\le f_j<\pi/8$. On overlapping caps, if $q_i<q_j$ then
$f_i-f_j=\varepsilon(q_j-q_i)>0$, so their graphs are disjoint.
Thus these are pairwise disjoint smooth spanning disks. The trivial
$n$-braid closes to the oriented $n$-component unlink; for $n=1$
this is the unknot.

At $n=0$ all strand and cycle unions are empty, every page has zero intersections,
and the closure is the empty link. The basepoint list and disk constructions
above then have no entries.

Let $F_n=\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle$ be the free group of
[[def-free-group]], identified with $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$ through the
standard meridians by
[[thm-the-punctured-disk-fundamental-group-is-free-on-standard-meridians]]. For
$1\le i\le n-1$, $\rho(\sigma_i)\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ is the automorphism
given on the basis by
$$\rho(\sigma_i)(x_i)=x_ix_{i+1}x_i^{-1},\qquad \rho(\sigma_i)(x_{i+1})=x_i, \qquad \rho(\sigma_i)(x_j)=x_j\ (j\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$
Its inverse is
$$\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_i)=x_{i+1},\qquad \rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_{i+1})=x_{i+1}^{-1}x_ix_{i+1},\qquad \rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_j)=x_j\ (j\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$
Products use ordinary function composition: the leftmost factor is the
outermost map and the rightmost factor acts first. Also
$\rho(\sigma_i^{-1}):=\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}$.

**The assignments are automorphisms, and the displayed formulas are inverse.**
By the universal property of the free group
([[def-free-group]], [[thm-reduced-words-form-the-free-group]]) the displayed
values on the free basis extend to a unique endomorphism
$\rho(\sigma_i):F_n\to F_n$, and likewise the displayed inverse formulas extend
to an endomorphism $\theta:F_n\to F_n$. Substituting,
$$\theta\bigl(\rho(\sigma_i)(x_i)\bigr)=\theta(x_ix_{i+1}x_i^{-1}) =\theta(x_i)\,\theta(x_{i+1})\,\theta(x_i)^{-1} =x_{i+1}\,\bigl(x_{i+1}^{-1}x_ix_{i+1}\bigr)\,x_{i+1}^{-1}=x_i,$$
$$\theta\bigl(\rho(\sigma_i)(x_{i+1})\bigr)=\theta(x_i)=x_{i+1},$$
and both composites fix every other basis element; so
$\theta\circ\rho(\sigma_i)=\operatorname{id}_{F_n}$ on a basis, hence as
endomorphisms. Symmetrically $\rho(\sigma_i)\circ\theta=
\operatorname{id}_{F_n}$. Therefore $\rho(\sigma_i)$ is a bijection with the
displayed inverse, i.e. an automorphism
([[def-group-isomorphism-and-automorphism]]).

**Convention note.** The displayed formulas are Artin's equations (14) and (15)
with the letter $\sigma_i$ and its inverse interchanged; under the frozen
geometric conventions of this library the *positive* half twist is the
anticlockwise supported half rotation (see
`def-elementary-geometric-half-twist` and
`thm-braid-group-is-the-boundary-fixed-mapping-class-group-of-the-punctured-disk`),
and
`prop-the-geometric-action-on-meridians-is-the-artin-representation` proves
that its action on the standard meridians is exactly the substitution frozen
above. The interchange is a convention, not a change of mathematical content:
$\rho$ and Artin's substitution generate the same subgroup of
$\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ and satisfy the same braid relations, and the
companion page shows that the mirror (clockwise) half rotation realizes
Artin's displayed formulas verbatim.

By [[lem-artin-automorphisms-satisfy-the-braid-relations]] the assignment
$\sigma_i\mapsto\rho(\sigma_i)$ satisfies the defining relations of the
presented braid group $B_n$ of
[[def-braid-group-by-the-artin-presentation]], so von Dyck's theorem
[[thm-von-dyck]] yields a unique homomorphism
$$\rho:B_n\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(F_n).$$
This is the **Artin representation**; it is the frozen convention for every
later statement of the page.

**Uniqueness and effectivity.** The homomorphism is unique because it is
prescribed on the generating set $\{\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}\}$, and it is
computed on a braid word by composing the finitely many automorphisms
$\rho(\sigma_i)^{\pm1}$ attached to its letters, as frozen in
[[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]]. No choice principle and no
geometric input are used in the construction; von Dyck's theorem
[[thm-von-dyck]] supplies existence and uniqueness of the extension.

Assume AC. Let $G_n$ be the geometric braid group,
$\varphi_n:B_n\to G_n$ the published surjection of
[[prop-the-artin-presentation-surjects-onto-geometric-braids]], and
$$\Psi:G_n\longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}(D^2,Q_n;\partial D^2)$$
the isomorphism of
[[thm-braid-group-is-the-boundary-fixed-mapping-class-group-of-the-punctured-disk]].
Identifying $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$ with $F_n$ by the standard meridians of
[[def-standard-meridians-of-a-punctured-disk]], the automorphism of $F_n$
induced by the mapping class $\Psi(\varphi_n(\beta))$ equals $\rho(\beta)$ for
every braid word $\beta$. In particular the geometric half twist $\sigma_i$ acts
as the Nielsen automorphism of
[[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]].

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $D^2=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|\le1\}$ and
$Q_n=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the closed unit disk and the base configuration of
[[def-boundary-fixed-mapping-class-group-of-a-punctured-disk]], so that
$q_1<\dots<q_n$ are distinct points of the real axis of
$\operatorname{int}D^2$. Fix the boundary basepoint
$$d:=(0,1)\in\partial D^2 .$$
For $1\le i\le n$ let $s_i\colon[0,1]\to D^2$ be the **straight stem**
$$s_i(t):=(1-t)\,d+t\,q_i ,$$
the straight segment from $d$ to $q_i$, and choose a round circle $C_i$ in
$D^2\setminus Q_n$ centred at $q_i$, of radius $0<\varepsilon_i<d(q_i,\partial D^2)$
so small that the closed disks $B_i$ bounded by the circles are pairwise disjoint, that each circle meets only its own stem, and that it meets $s_i$ exactly once, at
$p_i:=s_i(1-\varepsilon_i/L_i)$ where $L_i:=|d-q_i|$, and meets no other stem
$s_j$ with $j\ne i$. Write $c_i\colon[0,1]\to D^2\setminus Q_n$ for $C_i$
traversed once **positively** (counterclockwise), from $p_i$ back to $p_i$.
The **standard meridian loops** are the loops based at $d$
$$x_i:=s_i\,c_i\,s_i^{-1},\qquad 1\le i\le n,$$
read as $s_i$ from $d$ to $p_i$, then $c_i$, then $s_i$ from $p_i$ back to $d$
([[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]]). Further, $\partial$ denotes the
**positively oriented boundary loop**
$$\partial(t):=d\,e^{2\pi i t},\qquad t\in[0,1],$$
of $D^2$ based at $d$: it traverses $\partial D^2$ once counterclockwise,
starting and ending at $d$.

**Existence and independence of the choices.** The straight segments $s_i$
leave $d$ in pairwise distinct directions (the points $q_1,\dots,q_n$ are
distinct and lie strictly below $d$) and meet one another only at $d$; the
segments $s_i$ meet the real axis only at their endpoints $q_i$. An explicit choice-free family is given by
$$\varepsilon_i=\frac14\min\left(\{1-|q_i|\}\cup\left\{|q_i-q_j|,\frac{|q_i-q_j|}{\sqrt{1+q_j^2}}:j\ne i\right\}\right).$$
The finite set inside the minimum is nonempty and contains only positive
numbers. The distance from $q_i$ to the line through $d,q_j$ is
$|q_i-q_j|/\sqrt{1+q_j^2}$, so $B_i$ misses every other stem. Also
$\varepsilon_i+\varepsilon_j\le|q_i-q_j|/2<|q_i-q_j|$, proving disjointness
of the **closed** disks, and $\varepsilon_i<1-|q_i|$ keeps each disk inside
$D^2$. The radius is less than $|d-q_i|$, giving exactly the displayed contact
with its own stem. For $n=1$ the minimum has only its boundary-margin entry;
for $n=0$ the family is empty. Any family satisfying these conditions may be
fixed; this formula witnesses its existence without any choice axiom.

The class $[x_i]\in\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$ is independent of
all admissible radii, including the old broader convention requiring only
avoidance of the other stems. Such a circle encloses no $q_j$ with $j\ne i$:
otherwise the other stem from $d$, which lies outside the circle, to $q_j$
would cross it (or have $q_j$ on it). Thus the larger disk of any two admissible
concentric circles still contains no other puncture. Interpolate their radii
and their tether contact points radially; this is a based lasso homotopy in
$D^2\setminus Q_n$ ([[def-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy]]).
It does not require the intermediate circle to be disjoint from the other
circles, so the class argument does not circularly assume the newly explicit
representative convention. Fix once and
for all one such family of circles; every statement on this page uses that
fixed family.

**Frozen conventions of the page.** The stems and the basepoint transport are
fixed once and for all by the choices above; the stems are indexed so that the
positively oriented boundary loop $\partial$, as seen from $d$, meets the
directions of the stems in the order $s_1,s_2,\dots,s_n$. Products of braid
automorphisms use ordinary function composition: the leftmost factor is the
outermost map, so the rightmost factor acts first. No relation of the braid presentation and no choice principle
is used in this definition.

Let $F_n=\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle$ be the free group of
[[def-free-group]] on $n$ letters. The assignment $x_i\mapsto[x_i]$ extends to
a group isomorphism $F_n\to\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$; equivalently, the
classes $[x_1],\dots,[x_n]$ of the standard meridians of
[[def-standard-meridians-of-a-punctured-disk]] form a free basis of
$\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$.

Let $X$ be the based presentation $2$-complex with one vertex, oriented $1$-cells $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, and oriented $2$-cells attached along words $r_1,\ldots,r_m$ in the free group $F_n$. Let $G=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$ be its presented fundamental group, let $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$ be a representation, and let $\psi:G\to H$ be the declared free-abelian deck map. For $\Phi:\mathbb F[F_n]\to M_d(Q)$ induced by $x_j\mapsto\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)$, the twisted differential $\partial_1$ has blocks $\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)-I_d$, and the $i$th block row of $\partial_2$ is

$$\left(\Phi\left(\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial x_1}\right),\ldots,\Phi\left(\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial x_n}\right)\right),$$

where coefficient vectors are written as rows and differentials act on the right: the matrix of $\partial_1$ is the stacked column of blocks $\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)-I_d$, while the matrix of $\partial_2$ is the $md$-by-$nd$ block matrix whose $i$th row is the displayed Fox row. The Fox derivatives use the product and inverse recursions in the Wada definition. Thus the evaluated Fox-Jacobian blocks are exactly the cellular boundary blocks of the based twisted complex of this presentation $2$-complex.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L$ be a nonempty oriented smooth $r$-component link with $r\ge1$, compact exterior $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(L)$ obtained from pairwise-disjoint closed normal disk tubes, a finite oriented simplicial triangulation $K$ of $E_L$ with ordered vertices and simplices, with least vertex $v_0$ as the basepoint used in the cover definition, and one certified positive-meridian edge loop $\mu_i$ per component. Orient each normal disk so the positive tangent to its component followed by the positive disk basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$, and assume the resulting classes form the standard basis of $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$. If an integer-vector edge labeling is antisymmetric under edge reversal, sums to zero on every oriented 2-simplex, and evaluates to the $i$th standard basis vector on $\mu_i$, then the chain procedure returns a finite free chain complex over $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$. The first homology of this complex is the absolute maximal-abelian-cover Alexander module $A_L$. Its Fitting ideals are independent of the triangulation and cell lifts, and its order is defined up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

If $D$ is an integral domain, then $D\setminus\{0\}$ is multiplicative. Its localisation
$$ \operatorname{Frac}(D)=(D\setminus\{0\})^{-1}D $$
is the **field of fractions** of $D$. Thus its elements are fractions $a/b$ with $a,b\in D$ and $b\ne0$, modulo the localisation equivalence relation.

For every integral domain $D$, the localisation $\operatorname{Frac}(D)$ is a field. Its canonical map
$$ D\longrightarrow\operatorname{Frac}(D),\qquad d\longmapsto d/1, $$
is an injective unital ring homomorphism.

derivations.claim: Let $\alpha(g)=\rho(g)\psi(g)$ denote the coefficient matrix. Under [A1], the supplied filling certificate and [F7] identify $\pi_1(X)$ as the quotient of $\pi_1(Y)$ that kills the axis meridian $x$. Pulling the coefficient system back from $X$ therefore gives $\alpha(x)=I_d$ and $\psi(x)=1$; the core of $V$ is represented on $T$ by $g_n$, with matrix $M_n$. The algorithm forms the full positive-meridian basis on $X$ before applying $\chi$, while the compatible filling certificate specifies the resulting pulled-back or extended coefficient systems on $Y,T,V$ and makes them agree on overlaps. The chain-model theorem [F6] supplies the maximal-abelian-cover module computation on the full system; it does not prescribe the specialization order. The map $\pi_1(Y)\to\pi_1(X)$ is surjective, so the pulled-back deck map on $Y$ is still onto and the coefficient-unit images for the two exteriors agree. Since $D\ne0$, $M_n-I_d$ is invertible.

First compute the core-circle spine $V_{\mathrm{core}}$ with one $0$-cell and one $1$-cell for $g_n$. Its twisted boundary is $M_n-I_d$, so this core complex is acyclic and its torsion is $D^{-1}$. This core is not used as a CW pair containing $T$; a separate relative model and its torsion comparison are established before applying the gluing sequence. Give $T$ the standard one-vertex CW structure with $1$-cells $x,g_n$ and one commutator $2$-cell $xg_nx^{-1}g_n^{-1}$. The Fox boundary blocks are $d_1=(0,M_n-I_d)^\mathsf{T}$ and $d_2=(I_d-M_n,0)$: hence $d_1$ is onto, $d_2$ is injective onto $\ker d_1$, and $T$ is acyclic. In the torsion determinant product, the factors $\det(I_d-M_n)$ and $\det((M_n-I_d)^{-1})$ cancel up to $(-1)^d$, so $\tau(T)=(-1)^d$.

For $X$, Fox differentiation of $r_i=g_i^{-1}\beta_*(g_i)$ gives block row $M_i^{-1}(\widetilde B_{i,*}-e_i)$, where $e_i$ is the $i$th identity block row and $M_i=\rho(g_i)\psi(g_i)$. Thus, after deleting the $g_n$ column, the Fox block is $\operatorname{diag}(M_1^{-1},\ldots,M_{n-1}^{-1})(\overline B_\rho(\beta)-I)$, whose determinant is $\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\det(M_i^{-1})\right)N$. The prefactor is a nonzero coefficient unit. The $d_1$ block for $g_n$ is $M_n-I_d$, which is invertible, so $d_1$ is onto and projection from $\ker d_1$ to the first $n-1$ coordinate blocks is an isomorphism. By [F5], the projected $d_2$ is the displayed deleted Fox block. Therefore $N\ne0$ implies $d_2$ injective and, by dimensions and $d_1d_2=0$, the complex is acyclic; if the complex is acyclic, the same projection makes $d_2$ injective and forces $N\ne0$. Hence nonacyclicity is equivalent to $N=0$.

Give $D^2$ its boundary vertex, boundary edge $x$, and meridian disk cell $a$, and give $S^1$ its vertex and core edge $g_n$. Their product is a finite CW model $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ of the actual solid torus containing exactly the specified torus CW structure as its boundary subcomplex. Besides the cells of $T$, it has the $2$-cell $a\times\{*\}$, still denoted $a$, and the $3$-cell $b=a\times g_n$. Put $A=M_n-I_d$ and let $q$ denote the torus $2$-cell, with the orientation in step 2.1. For a coefficient row $v$, the product boundaries are $$\partial a(v)=x(v),\qquad \partial q(v)=x(-vA),\qquad \partial b(v)=q(v)+a(vA).$$ The first formula is the meridian disk boundary, the second is the torus Fox boundary from step 2.1, and the third is the oriented boundary of disk times core edge; its two terms have cancelling images under $\partial$. Replace the degree-two block $q(v)$ by $q'(v)=q(v)+a(vA)$. This block-triangular basis change has determinant one, $\partial q'=0$, and $\partial b(v)=q'(v)$. Split off the unit two-term pair $(b,q')$, then the unit pair $(a,x)$. The remaining based complex is exactly the core complex with $\partial g_n(v)=vA$. Each split pair has identity incidence and torsion one up to the sign unit, and the triangular change contributes determinant one. Hence $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ has the same homology and torsion class as $V_{\mathrm{core}}$, so it is acyclic and its torsion is $D^{-1}$ up to the declared units. This calculation supplies the missing based comparison while retaining $T$ in the actual gluing model.

Use the relative-cellular gluing operation [F9] for the actual decomposition in the supplied certificate. For $V$ use $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ from step 3.1, not its core spine. For the exterior pieces the operation uses the compatible relative CW representatives and the supplied based simple-spine comparisons. Equivalently, a boundary map into a spine is represented by its finite cellular mapping cylinder: each added prism over a torus cell pairs with its source face, with lifted incidence a unit; these pairs are removed in decreasing cell dimension. Their torsion changes lie in the declared unit subgroup. Thus the based torsion classes used below are those of the supplied spines, without identifying the boundary torus with a subcomplex of a core circle or of an abstract presentation. In the common relative models each cell of $T$ occurs in both pieces, and each other cell occurs in exactly one. Inclusion into the first piece and its negative into the second, followed by the difference quotient to the union, therefore give the degreewise split short exact sequence $$0\longrightarrow C_*(T)\longrightarrow C_*(Y_{\mathrm{rel}})\oplus C_*(V_{\mathrm{rel}})\longrightarrow C_*(X_{\mathrm{rel}})\longrightarrow0.$$ Choose the shared lifts compatibly; any permitted adjustment changes only the declared determinant/deck units. Since $T$ and $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ are acyclic by steps 2.1 and 3.1, the long exact homology sequence identifies $H_*(Y;Q^d)$ with $H_*(X;Q^d)$. Thus $Y$ is acyclic exactly when $X$ is. Subsequent references to the gluing sequence mean these relative models and their certified based comparisons.

In the acyclic case, choose boundary bases in the short exact sequence compatibly: lift a basis of each quotient boundary space, append a basis of the subcomplex boundary space, and lift the resulting boundary bases to chain groups. The change-of-basis matrices are block triangular with diagonal blocks the matrices for the subcomplex and quotient, so their determinants multiply degree by degree; the alternating torsion product therefore gives $\tau(Y)\tau(V)=\pm\tau(T)\tau(X)$. As $\tau(T)=\pm1$ and both signs lie in the declared unit subgroup, step 2.1 yields $\tau(Y)\doteq\tau(X)D$.

Suppose $X$ and hence $Y$ are acyclic over $Q$. The finite based chain modules over $\Lambda=\mathbb F[H]$ are free. If $z\in C_1(Y;\Lambda^d)$ is a $1$-cycle, acyclicity over $Q$ gives $z/1=d_2(y)/s$ for some $y\in C_2(Y;\Lambda^d)$ and nonzero $s\in\Lambda$. By [F8], equality in the fraction field means that some nonzero $u\in\Lambda$ annihilates $sz-d_2(y)$; since $C_1(Y;\Lambda^d)$ is free over the domain $\Lambda$, multiplication by $u$ is injective, so $sz=d_2(y)$. Every degree-one homology class is therefore killed by a nonzero element of $\Lambda$.

Apply [F2] to the certified spine of $Y$ and delete the $g_n$ column, whose denominator is $D\ne0$. For $s_i=\beta_*(g_i)(x^{-1}g_ix)^{-1}$, the $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ Fox blocks evaluate to $\widetilde B-I$, where $\widetilde B$ is the full cumulative-meridian Fox matrix, and the $x$-column blocks are $I_d-M_i$ with $M_i=\rho(g_i)\psi(g_i)$. Because $\beta_*(g_n)=g_n$, the last row of $\widetilde B-I$ is zero; after deleting its $g_n$ column, the remaining matrix has upper-left block $\overline B_\rho(\beta)-I$, arbitrary upper-right block, zero lower-left block, and lower-right block $I_d-M_n$. It is block upper triangular, so its determinant is $(-1)^dND$. Dividing by $D$ gives $(-1)^dN$, which represents $N$ modulo the sign unit. Consequently $\tau(Y)\doteq N$.

If the complex is acyclic, combine steps 5.1 and 6.1 to obtain $\tau(X)D\doteq N$, hence $\tau(X)\doteq N/D$. If it is nonacyclic, step 2.2 gives $N=0$, and the declared convention sets $\tau(X)=0=N/D$. This proves the statement in both branches.
