The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, and let $F,F'$ be any connected compact smooth oriented spanning surfaces for $K$. For any ordered integral bases of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and $H_1(F';\mathbb Z)$, the matrices of the positive-push Seifert pairing are related by a finite sequence of integral unimodular congruences and the two rank-two elementary Seifert enlargements or their reverses.

Let $V$ be an even-order square matrix with integer entries, of size $n=2g$. A unimodular congruence replaces $V$ by $P^TVP$ for an integer matrix $P$ with determinant $+1$ or $-1$. For $x,y\in\mathbb Z^n$ as column vectors and $z\in\mathbb Z$, the two elementary enlargements of $V$ are
$$
E_0(V;x,y,z)=\begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&0\\0^T&1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
E_1(V;x,y,z)=\begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&1\\0^T&0&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Two even-order integral matrices are **S-equivalent** if one can be obtained from the other by a finite sequence of unimodular congruences, elementary enlargements, and reverse elementary enlargements.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented surface with oriented boundary $K$, let $V$ be the matrix of the Seifert pairing $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ in an ordered integral basis, and let $\omega\in S^1\setminus\{1\}$. Define the **Levine–Tristram Hermitian matrix** by
$$H_\omega(V)=(1-\omega)V+(1-\bar\omega)V^T.$$
It is Hermitian because $V$ is real and $\bar\omega=\omega^{-1}$. Its signature is the number of positive eigenvalues minus the number of negative eigenvalues, both counted with multiplicity and with zero eigenvalues omitted. When $\Delta_K(\omega)\ne0$, define $\sigma_\omega(K)$ to be this signature. At a root $\omega_0\ne1$ of $\Delta_K$, define $\sigma_{\omega_0}(K)$ to be the arithmetic mean of the two one-sided limits of $\sigma_{e^{i\theta}}(K)$ as $\theta$ approaches an argument of $\omega_0$ from below and above. The invariance and one-sided-existence lemmas justify treating these values as independent of the chosen surface and basis.

Assume the hypotheses and conventions of the Levine–Tristram form definition. At every root $\omega_0\in S^1\setminus\{1\}$ of $\Delta_K$, each one-sided limit of the nonroot signature as the parameter moves along the unit circle to $\omega_0$ exists and is an integer.

derivations.claim: Since $P$ is real, $H_\omega(P^TVP)=P^TH_\omega(V)P$. An invertible congruence is a change of coordinates in the associated Hermitian form, so its positive and negative indices are unchanged: a maximal positive subspace maps bijectively by $P$, and likewise for negative subspaces. Hence the signature is invariant under basis change.

Put $c=1-\omega\ne0$. For either enlargement, the enlarged Hermitian matrix has block form
$$\widetilde H=\begin{pmatrix}H&b&0\\b^*&z(c+\bar c)&\lambda\\0&\bar\lambda&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad |\lambda|=|c|>0,$$
where $H=H_\omega(V)$, $b$ is the column determined by the enlargement vectors, and $z\in\mathbb Z$. The lower $2\times2$ block $D$ has determinant $-|c|^2<0$, hence one positive and one negative eigenvalue. Its inverse has $(D^{-1})_{11}=0$. The block congruence eliminating $b$ therefore has Schur complement $H-b(D^{-1})_{11}b^*=H$, so $\widetilde H$ is congruent to $H\oplus D$. The block $D$ contributes signature $0$, proving enlargement invariance for every $\omega\ne1$, including singular parameters.

By [F1], any two knot matrices are connected by the operations of steps 1.1 and 2.1, so their signatures agree at every nonroot parameter. The one-sided signatures are equal as functions on each punctured neighboring arc; by [F3] their arithmetic averages are defined and agree at a root as well. Reductions reverse the same equalities.

Order the two cores $a,b$ with the positive Hopf core first, orient them so $a\cdot_F b=+1$, and use the standard plumbing side for which $a^+$ bounds a disk disjoint from $b$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Use the upper half-space model
$$
\mathbb H^3=\{(x+iy,t):x,y\in\mathbb R,\ t>0\},\qquad
ds^2=t^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2+dt^2),
$$
whose ideal boundary is $\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$. An oriented ideal tetrahedron in normalized position has ideal vertices $0,1,\infty,z$, where $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Its three edge-shape parameters are
$$
z,\qquad z'=\frac1{1-z},\qquad z''=\frac{z-1}{z},
$$
each assigned to one pair of opposite edges; the parameter at a corner of a truncated ideal vertex triangle is the parameter of the incident edge. For an oriented path $\gamma$ in a triangulated torus link of ideal vertices, its cusp multiplier $H(\gamma)$ is the product of the corner parameters encountered along $\gamma$, using the parameter when the path cuts off that corner on its left and its reciprocal when it cuts off the corner on its right.

derivations.claim: Since $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, the imaginary parts of $z$, $z'=1/(1-z)$ and $z''=1-1/z$ are all positive: the second is $\operatorname{Im}z/|1-z|^2$, and the third is $\operatorname{Im}z/|z|^2$. Thus their principal arguments lie in $(0,\pi)$.

Multiplication gives $zz'z''=z\cdot(1-z)^{-1}\cdot(z-1)z^{-1}=-1$. The sum of the three arguments is therefore an odd multiple of $\pi$; because it lies strictly between $0$ and $3\pi$, it must equal $\pi$. The arguments are the dihedral angles by the edge cross-ratio convention in [F1].

For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, $1-\omega=\omega^{-1}$ and $\omega-1=\omega^2$. Hence $1/(1-\omega)=\omega$ and $(\omega-1)/\omega=\omega$; each parameter has argument $\pi/3$. Each of the three parameter arguments occurs on a pair of opposite edges, proving the regular-angle assertion.

For real $\theta$, define the Lobachevsky function
$$
\Lambda(\theta)=-\int_0^\theta \log|2\sin u|\,du,
$$
where the integral is interpreted improperly at zeros of $\sin u$.

For every real $\theta$, $\Lambda$ is continuous, odd, and $\pi$-periodic, with $\Lambda(\pi/2)=0$ and
$$
\Lambda(2\theta)=2\Lambda(\theta)+2\Lambda(\theta+\pi/2).
$$
For $0\le\theta\le\pi$,
$$
\Lambda(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sin(2n\theta)}{n^2}.
$$
In particular,
$$
\Lambda(\pi/3)=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).
$$
For every integer $N\ge1$, the positive remainder after the terms $k=0,\ldots,N$ is at most $\sqrt3/(72N^2)$.

Set $x=\cos\theta$, so $\zeta\le\theta\le\pi/2$. Sine addition identities change the logarithm ratio to $\sin(\theta+\zeta)/\sin(\theta-\zeta)$, and therefore $\operatorname{Vol}(\mathcal O_\zeta)=\frac14\int_\zeta^{\pi/2}\log\frac{\sin(\theta+\zeta)}{\sin(\theta-\zeta)}\,d\theta=\frac14(\Lambda(2\zeta)-\Lambda(\pi/2+\zeta)+\Lambda(\pi/2-\zeta))$. If $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(M)$ had nontrivial kernel, [F1] would supply an essential simple curve in $T$ bounding a proper disk in $M$, contradicting boundary incompressibility. Hence $\pi_1(M)$ contains the injected group $\pi_1(T)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ and is infinite.

The given embedded-torus atoroidality and the hypothesis that $M$ is not Seifert-fibered allow [F2] to be applied. Therefore every $\pi_1$-injective torus map is homotopic into $\partial M$. All hypotheses of [F3] now hold for this actual $M$, so $\operatorname{int}(M)$ admits a complete finite-volume metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$. This applies to fibered knot exteriors as well as nonfibered ones; no additional non-interval-bundle assumption has been introduced.

The interior of a compact connected manifold with one connected boundary component has one end: a boundary collar gives a cofinal family of connected complements of compact subsets, namely $T\times(0,\epsilon)$. By [F4], every end of the metric from step 1.2 is a rank-two horoball quotient, so there is exactly one torus cusp. It belongs to the unique original boundary end. This is an existence assertion for a metric on the original interior; no prescribed horosphere scale, meridian–longitude translation vectors, or separately marked peripheral conjugacy is asserted. No conclusion is used outside the four topological hypotheses of the Statement.

citations.quote:
Use the upper half-space model
$$
\mathbb H^3=\{(x+iy,t):x,y\in\mathbb R,\ t>0\},\qquad
ds^2=t^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2+dt^2),
$$
whose ideal boundary is $\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$. An oriented ideal tetrahedron in normalized position has ideal vertices $0,1,\infty,z$, where $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Its three edge-shape parameters are
$$
z,\qquad z'=\frac1{1-z},\qquad z''=\frac{z-1}{z},
$$
each assigned to one pair of opposite edges; the parameter at a corner of a truncated ideal vertex triangle is the parameter of the incident edge. For an oriented path $\gamma$ in a triangulated torus link of ideal vertices, its cusp multiplier $H(\gamma)$ is the product of the corner parameters encountered along $\gamma$, using the parameter when the path cuts off that corner on its left and its reciprocal when it cuts off the corner on its right.

For an oriented ideal tetrahedron with normalized vertices $0,1,\infty,z$ and $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its three edge-shape parameters are $z$, $z'=1/(1-z)$, and $z''=(z-1)/z$. They satisfy $zz'z''=-1$, and their arguments in $(0,\pi)$ are the three dihedral angles, whose sum is $\pi$. For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, the choice $z=\omega$ gives $z=z'=z''=\omega$ and all six dihedral angles equal to $\pi/3$.

Let an orientable finite ideal triangulation have exactly one ideal vertex, whose link is a torus. Suppose its tetrahedra carry positive shapes whose edge products equal $1$ and whose dihedral angles sum to $2\pi$ around every edge. If the cusp multipliers $H(\alpha)$ and $H(\beta)$ are $1$ for a basis $\alpha,\beta$ of the torus fundamental group, then the glued hyperbolic metric is complete at that cusp.

Let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb C$ be a rank-two lattice acting on $\mathbb H^3$ by horizontal translations, and let
$$
C=\{(x+iy,t):t\ge1\}/\Gamma
$$
be the quotient of the horoball $t\ge1$. If $A$ is the Euclidean area of a fundamental parallelogram for $\Gamma$, then the end is at infinite hyperbolic distance and $\operatorname{Vol}(C)=A/2$.

Every regular ideal tetrahedron in hyperbolic three-space has volume
$$
v_3=3\Lambda(\pi/3)
=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).
$$

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume countable choice. For a smooth oriented knot with a chosen product tubular neighbourhood $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$, let $\mu$ be the positive fibre meridian and let $\sigma$ be the product section $s\mapsto(s,1)$ of $T_K=\partial N(K)\cong S^1\times S^1$. Then $T_K=\partial E_K$ is a torus and $[\mu],[\sigma]$ form a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. The curve $\sigma$ is a product section; this statement does not assert that it is the preferred zero-homology longitude.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]], with $h=\frac{1}{4(n+1)}$ and
$q_j=((2j-n-1)h,0)$. Fix an index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$. The two adjacent
base points are

$$q_i=\bigl((2i-n-1)h,0\bigr),\qquad q_{i+1}=\bigl((2i+1-n)h,0\bigr),$$

their **midpoint** is $m_i:=(q_i+q_{i+1})/2=((2i-n)h,0)=q_i+(h,0)$, and their
**support disc** is the open disc

$$U_i:=\bigl\{w\in\mathbb R^2:\lVert w-m_i\rVert_2<\tfrac32h\bigr\}.$$

The support disc contains the two base points $q_i,q_{i+1}$, whose distance from
$m_i$ is $h$, and it contains no other base point: for $k<i$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(i-k)+1)h\ge 3h$ and for $k>i+1$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(k-i)-1)h\ge3h$, both exceeding $\tfrac32h$. Moreover
$U_i\subseteq D^\circ$, because every point of $U_i$ has norm at most
$\lVert m_i\rVert_2+\tfrac32h\le(n-2)h+\tfrac32h<(n+1)h<1$. Finally
$U_i\cap U_j=\varnothing$ whenever $|i-j|>1$, since then the midpoints are at
distance $2|i-j|h\ge4h>3h$, twice the radius.

**The positive half twist.** Define $\rho\colon I\to\mathbb R^2$, the
**anticlockwise diamond path**, by

$$\rho(t):=\begin{cases}\bigl(2th-h,\,-2th\bigr),&0\le t\le \tfrac12,\\[2pt] \bigl(2th-h,\,2th-2h\bigr),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$

Thus $\rho(0)=(-h,0)$, $\rho(\tfrac12)=(0,-h)$, $\rho(1)=(h,0)$, and $\rho$ is
continuous, piecewise linear, and satisfies $\lVert\rho(t)\rVert_2\le h$ for all
$t$ with $\rho(t)\neq0$ throughout. The **elementary half twist at $i$**, written
$\sigma_i$, is the tuple of motions

$$(\sigma_i)_i(t):=m_i+\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_k(t):=q_k\ \ (k\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$

It is a braid based at $Q$
([[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]],
[[def-continuous-map-top]]): the two moving points stay in $U_i$ and are
antipodal about $m_i$, so they are distinct; every other point is fixed and lies
outside $U_i$; and the endpoint permutation is the transposition of $i$ and
$i+1$, since $(\sigma_i)_i(1)=m_i+(h,0)=q_{i+1}$ and
$(\sigma_i)_{i+1}(1)=m_i-(h,0)=q_i$.

The words *positive* and *anticlockwise* refer to the fixed orientation of the
plane of the disc and to the fixed planar projection whose horizontal axis
contains $Q$: the moving pair turns through the half turn anticlockwise, the
label $i$ passing below its midpoint and the label $i+1$ above. Together with
the first-under-second stacking convention of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]] this fixes the sign
convention for every signed crossing on this page and its companion.

**The opposite half twist.** The **opposite** (clockwise) half twist at $i$ is
defined by the reflected path

$$\rho^{-}(t):=\bigl(\rho_1(t),-\rho_2(t)\bigr),$$

through the motions $(\sigma_i^{-})_i(t):=m_i+\rho^{-}(t)$,
$(\sigma_i^{-})_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho^{-}(t)$ and
$(\sigma_i^{-})_k(t):=q_k$ for $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$. It is again a braid supported
in $U_i$ with endpoint permutation the transposition of $i$ and $i+1$; its pair
turns through the same half turn clockwise, the label $i$ passing above the
midpoint. The two motions are not equal, and they are not related by a
reparametrisation of the height: they are the two signed crossings of the pair.

**The opposite motion is the group inverse.** For a braid $\beta$ the reversed
braid $\overline\beta_j(t)=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)$ represents
$[\beta]^{-1}$ in the group $G_n$
([[thm-geometric-braids-form-a-group]]). For $\beta=\sigma_i$ one computes
$\overline{\sigma_i}=\sigma_i^{-}$: reversing the height and relabelling by the
transposition of $i$ and $i+1$ sends $\rho(t)=m_i+(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ to the
motion with relative path $-\rho(1-t)$, which is the reflected path
$\rho^-$ traversed from $t=0$ to $t=1$. Hence

$$[\sigma_i^{-}]=[\sigma_i]^{-1}\qquad\text{in }G_n .$$

**Elementary cases.** For $n\le1$ there is no index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$,
and there are no elementary half twists; the assertions above are vacuous. For
$n\ge2$ and $1\le i\le n-1$ both $[\sigma_i]$ and $[\sigma_i^{-}]$ are
nonidentity elements of $G_n$, since their endpoint permutations are
transpositions, which are not the identity permutation.

**Two letters do not commute in general.** For adjacent indices the supports
$U_i$ and $U_{i+1}$ overlap and no commutation is asserted;
[[lem-geometric-far-commutativity]] proves commutativity only for disjoint
supports.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]]. Write

$$G_n:=\{[\beta]:\beta\ \text{a braid based at}\ Q\}$$

for the set of braid isotopy classes relative to the top and bottom
([[def-braid-isotopy-relative-top-and-bottom]]), and let $[\gamma][\beta]:
=[\gamma\star\beta]$ be the stacking of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]]. Then:

**(a)** $G_n$ is a group ([[def-group]]) with this operation. Its identity is
the class $[e]$ of the trivial braid $e_j(t):=q_j$, and the inverse of
$[\beta]$, for $\beta=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ with endpoint permutation $\pi(\beta)$,
is the class of the **reversed braid**

$$\overline\beta_j(t):=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)\qquad(t\in I,\ 1\le j\le n).$$

**(b)** The endpoint permutation map

$$\pi\colon G_n\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad[\beta]\longmapsto\pi(\beta),$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]).

The construction is choice-free: all motions and reparametrisations used are
given by explicit formulas.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $\beta=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a geometric braid with
the fixed real basepoints $q_j=((2j-n-1)/(4(n+1)),0)$ and endpoint
permutation $\pi$, as in [[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]].
Identify the disk with $\{x\in\mathbb C:|x|<1\}$ and put
$$V=(D^\circ\times[0,1])/((x,1)\sim(x,0)).$$
The quotient and its topology use [[def-product-topology]] and the circle
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of [[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]].
The interval images
$$s_j=\{[(z_j(t),t)]:0\le t\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\beta)=\bigcup_{j=1}^n s_j$$
are the **closure in the open solid torus**. In general an individual
$s_j$ is an interval image, not a closed circle: its last point is the
first point of $s_{\pi(j)}$.

**Components and orientation.** For a cycle
$(j,\pi(j),\ldots,\pi^{k-1}(j))$ concatenate these $k$ strand maps in
that order, with parameter in $[0,k]$. Their endpoints agree in $V$,
so the concatenation factors through $\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$.
It is injective on this circle: points at distinct nonintegral heights
can agree only when their parameters have the same fractional part,
and the distinct strands at that height have distinct disk coordinates;
at integral heights only the specified adjacent endpoints agree.
Thus each cycle gives an embedded circle. Different cycles give
disjoint circles, and every strand belongs to exactly one cycle.
These circles are precisely the connected components of the closure.
The orientation is increasing concatenation parameter. In particular
the number of components equals the number of cycles of $\pi$.

**The standard axis and fixed framing.** In
$S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, as in
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], set
$$A=\{(0,w):|w|=1\},\qquad P_\theta=\{(z,w)\in S^3:z\ne0,\ \arg z=\theta\}.$$
Fix the following particular diffeomorphism, including its disk framing:
$$\varphi([(x,t)])=  \bigl(\sqrt{1-|x|^2}\,e^{2\pi it},x\bigr):  V\longrightarrow S^3\setminus A.$$
Its inverse has disk coordinate $x=w$ and circle coordinate
$[t]=[\arg z/(2\pi)]$. Every $P_\theta$ is consequently an open disk.
The **raw topological oriented closure** is
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{top}}=\varphi(\operatorname{cl}(\beta)).$$
This explicit $\varphi$ is part of the construction; the definition
does not allow an arbitrary page-preserving change of framing.

**Page intersections and smooth representatives.** The whole closure
meets every page in exactly $n$ points. A component belonging to a
$\pi$-cycle of length $k$ meets each page in exactly $k$ points:
at any fractional height it uses exactly those $k$ distinct strands.
The page coordinate of its concatenation is $[t]$, for
$t\in\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$, so its oriented degree is $+k$.
If all disk-coordinate strand maps are smooth and have all positive-order derivatives
zero at their endpoints, their cycle concatenations have matching jets
at every seam. The page coordinate has nonzero derivative, so the
result is a smooth embedding of disjoint oriented circles, in the
sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. For an endpoint-flat smooth braid, its literal $\varphi$-image is therefore a smooth oriented link and is denoted $\widehat\beta$.

**Closure in the smooth oriented-link category.** The raw image need not be smooth, even if individual strands are smooth but their endpoint jets fail to match at the cycle seams. For an arbitrary continuous braid, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) and choose a smooth representative $\beta_s$ by [[lem-every-geometric-braid-is-braid-isotopic-to-a-smooth-braid]]. Make it endpoint-flat by composing all disk-coordinate strands with a fixed smooth nondecreasing $\psi:I\to I$, equal to $0$ near $0$ and $1$ near $1$. Interpolation of height maps $(1-u)t+u\psi(t)$ is an endpoint-fixed braid isotopy, because every strand is evaluated at the same height. The smooth-category closure of $\beta$ is the oriented-link isotopy class of this chosen model's literal $\varphi$-image; when a subset is needed, use that chosen closed-braid representative. Independence of the representative is proved by [[lem-closure-depends-only-on-the-braid-isotopy-class]]. Page and cycle properties refer to the chosen constructed closed braid, with the same number of strands and endpoint permutation as $\beta$.

If $\beta$ already has smooth strands with matching cycle-seam jets, in particular if it is endpoint-flat, its literal raw image is a smooth link and is retained as $\widehat\beta$. The raw quotient, fixed $\varphi$, finite cycles, page counts and trivial closures remain choice-free. Finite elementary words have explicit smooth endpoint-flat models, so forming their literal closures also requires no choice assumption; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used for the general continuous-representative convention and its independence theorem.

**The trivial closure.** For the constant braid its circles are
$\{(\sqrt{1-q_j^2}e^{2\pi it},q_j):[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\}$.
They are latitudes of the sphere
$S=\{(z,w)\in S^3:\operatorname{Im}w=0\}$, with
$\operatorname{Re}w=q_j$. Each northern cap
$C_j=\{p\in S:\operatorname{Re}w(p)\ge q_j\}$ is a smooth disk:
stereographic coordinates on $S$ give radius
$\sqrt{(1-q_j)/(1+q_j)}$ for this cap. To make their spanning disks
disjoint, let $e$ be the unit vector in the $\operatorname{Im}w$
direction, set $\varepsilon=\pi/16$ and
$f_j(p)=\varepsilon(\operatorname{Re}w(p)-q_j)$ on $C_j$, and use
$$F_j(p)=\cos(f_j(p))p+\sin(f_j(p))e.$$
The boundary is fixed. The tubular parametrization
$(p,s)\mapsto\cos(s)p+\sin(s)e$ is injective for $|s|<\pi/2$,
and $0\le f_j<\pi/8$. On overlapping caps, if $q_i<q_j$ then
$f_i-f_j=\varepsilon(q_j-q_i)>0$, so their graphs are disjoint.
Thus these are pairwise disjoint smooth spanning disks. The trivial
$n$-braid closes to the oriented $n$-component unlink; for $n=1$
this is the unknot.

At $n=0$ all strand and cycle unions are empty, every page has zero intersections,
and the closure is the empty link. The basepoint list and disk constructions
above then have no entries.

derivations.claim: The endpoint permutation of $(\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1})^2$ is $(12)(23)(12)(23)=(1\ 3\ 2)$, because each half twist has the adjacent transposition as endpoint permutation and inverse has the same transposition. By [F8], its closure is one component. Cut the standard four-crossing figure-eight diagram along its projection regions and four crossing arcs. Above and below the diagram this produces two ideal balls: each crossing arc has four face-side copies, and every face is a diagram region. Gluing upper and lower faces with the same region label restores the cut-open complement, because each cut face and crossing-arc side is identified with exactly its original mate; the only unfilled points are the deleted knot arcs, which are ideal vertices. Collapsing the two bigon faces gives two tetrahedra. Recording the vertex matches on their four faces gives exactly the four maps in the statement.

By [F2], at $z_1=z_2=z_3=w_1=w_2=w_3=\omega$ every edge parameter is $\omega$. The first edge class has product $\omega^6=1$, and the second has product $\omega^6=1$; each class contains six edge copies, so its total dihedral angle is $6(\pi/3)=2\pi$.

Applying the four vertex maps identifies all eight tetrahedron vertices into one ideal vertex and the twelve tetrahedron edges into the two six-edge classes in the statement. To check the link vertices explicitly, write $u|v$ for the truncation corner at ideal vertex $u$ on edge $uv$. The four corner classes are $\{0|1,0|2,3|2,3'|1',3'|2',0'|1'\}$, $\{1|0,1'|3',2|0,2'|3',1'|0',2|3\}$, $\{1|2,1'|2',0|3,0'|2',1|3,0'|3'\}$, and $\{2|1,2'|1',3|0,2'|0',3|1,3'|0'\}$; these are disjoint and contain all $24$ link corners. The eight link triangles have their $24$ sides identified in $12$ pairs, so $\chi=4-12+8=0$. The four face maps give a connected adjacency graph on the eight link triangles; their induced boundary-orientation signs are respectively negative, negative, negative, negative. Hence the link is connected, closed and orientable, and therefore is a torus.

Tracking the stated eight-triangle strip across the four face pairings closes each listed path. Cut the strip open along $\alpha$: the $\beta$ path becomes an arc joining the two copies of that cut, and the face table shows it crosses the cut once, from the negative to the positive side. Thus the single signed intersection is $+1$; on a torus this makes $([\alpha],[\beta])$ a homology basis. Since $\pi_1(T)=\mathbb Z^2$ and its abelianization is $H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$, these loops also generate $\pi_1(T)$. Substituting the regular shape into the listed corner products gives $H(\alpha)=((\omega\omega)/(\omega\omega))^2=1$ and $H(\beta)=\omega/\omega=1$.

The edge conditions in step 1.2, torus link in step 2.1, and basis cusp multipliers in step 3.1 satisfy [F3], so the glued metric is complete at its unique torus cusp. The face maps are hyperbolic face isometries; the $2\pi$ edge-angle sums make the metric smooth across every edge, and the only omitted locus is the single ideal vertex. Thus completeness at this cusp is completeness of the whole glued complement. Each tetrahedron has volume $v_3$ by [F5], so additivity gives total volume $2v_3<\infty$; its horospherical cusp truncation also has finite volume by [F4]. The induced metric on the figure-eight complement is therefore complete and finite-volume with one peripheral torus cusp.

citations.quote:
Use the upper half-space model
$$\mathbb H^3=\{(x+iy,t):x,y\in\mathbb R,\ t>0\},\qquad ds^2=t^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2+dt^2),$$
whose ideal boundary is $\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$. An oriented ideal tetrahedron in normalized position has ideal vertices $0,1,\infty,z$, where $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Its three edge-shape parameters are
$$z,\qquad z'=\frac1{1-z},\qquad z''=\frac{z-1}{z},$$
each assigned to one pair of opposite edges; the parameter at a corner of a truncated ideal vertex triangle is the parameter of the incident edge. For an oriented path $\gamma$ in a triangulated torus link of ideal vertices, its cusp multiplier $H(\gamma)$ is the product of the corner parameters encountered along $\gamma$, using the parameter when the path cuts off that corner on its left and its reciprocal when it cuts off the corner on its right.

For an oriented ideal tetrahedron with normalized vertices $0,1,\infty,z$ and $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its three edge-shape parameters are $z$, $z'=1/(1-z)$, and $z''=(z-1)/z$. They satisfy $zz'z''=-1$, and their arguments in $(0,\pi)$ are the three dihedral angles, whose sum is $\pi$. For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, the choice $z=\omega$ gives $z=z'=z''=\omega$ and all six dihedral angles equal to $\pi/3$.

Let an orientable finite ideal triangulation have exactly one ideal vertex, whose link is a torus. Suppose its tetrahedra carry positive shapes whose edge products equal $1$ and whose dihedral angles sum to $2\pi$ around every edge. If the cusp multipliers $H(\alpha)$ and $H(\beta)$ are $1$ for a basis $\alpha,\beta$ of the torus fundamental group, then the glued hyperbolic metric is complete at that cusp.

Let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb C$ be a rank-two lattice acting on $\mathbb H^3$ by horizontal translations, and let
$$
C=\{(x+iy,t):t\ge1\}/\Gamma
$$
be the quotient of the horoball $t\ge1$. If $A$ is the Euclidean area of a fundamental parallelogram for $\Gamma$, then the end is at infinite hyperbolic distance and $\operatorname{Vol}(C)=A/2$.

Every regular ideal tetrahedron in hyperbolic three-space has volume
$$v_3=3\Lambda(\pi/3) =\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).$$

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume countable choice. For a smooth oriented knot with a chosen product tubular neighbourhood $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$, let $\mu$ be the positive fibre meridian and let $\sigma$ be the product section $s\mapsto(s,1)$ of $T_K=\partial N(K)\cong S^1\times S^1$. Then $T_K=\partial E_K$ is a torus and $[\mu],[\sigma]$ form a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. The curve $\sigma$ is a product section; this statement does not assert that it is the preferred zero-homology longitude.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]], with $h=\frac{1}{4(n+1)}$ and
$q_j=((2j-n-1)h,0)$. Fix an index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$. The two adjacent
base points are

$$q_i=\bigl((2i-n-1)h,0\bigr),\qquad q_{i+1}=\bigl((2i+1-n)h,0\bigr),$$

their **midpoint** is $m_i:=(q_i+q_{i+1})/2=((2i-n)h,0)=q_i+(h,0)$, and their
**support disc** is the open disc

$$U_i:=\bigl\{w\in\mathbb R^2:\lVert w-m_i\rVert_2<\tfrac32h\bigr\}.$$

The support disc contains the two base points $q_i,q_{i+1}$, whose distance from
$m_i$ is $h$, and it contains no other base point: for $k<i$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(i-k)+1)h\ge 3h$ and for $k>i+1$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(k-i)-1)h\ge3h$, both exceeding $\tfrac32h$. Moreover
$U_i\subseteq D^\circ$, because every point of $U_i$ has norm at most
$\lVert m_i\rVert_2+\tfrac32h\le(n-2)h+\tfrac32h<(n+1)h<1$. Finally
$U_i\cap U_j=\varnothing$ whenever $|i-j|>1$, since then the midpoints are at
distance $2|i-j|h\ge4h>3h$, twice the radius.

**The positive half twist.** Define $\rho\colon I\to\mathbb R^2$, the
**anticlockwise diamond path**, by

$$\rho(t):=\begin{cases}\bigl(2th-h,\,-2th\bigr),&0\le t\le \tfrac12,\\[2pt] \bigl(2th-h,\,2th-2h\bigr),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$

Thus $\rho(0)=(-h,0)$, $\rho(\tfrac12)=(0,-h)$, $\rho(1)=(h,0)$, and $\rho$ is
continuous, piecewise linear, and satisfies $\lVert\rho(t)\rVert_2\le h$ for all
$t$ with $\rho(t)\neq0$ throughout. The **elementary half twist at $i$**, written
$\sigma_i$, is the tuple of motions

$$(\sigma_i)_i(t):=m_i+\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_k(t):=q_k\ \ (k\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$

It is a braid based at $Q$
([[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]],
[[def-continuous-map-top]]): the two moving points stay in $U_i$ and are
antipodal about $m_i$, so they are distinct; every other point is fixed and lies
outside $U_i$; and the endpoint permutation is the transposition of $i$ and
$i+1$, since $(\sigma_i)_i(1)=m_i+(h,0)=q_{i+1}$ and
$(\sigma_i)_{i+1}(1)=m_i-(h,0)=q_i$.

The words *positive* and *anticlockwise* refer to the fixed orientation of the
plane of the disc and to the fixed planar projection whose horizontal axis
contains $Q$: the moving pair turns through the half turn anticlockwise, the
label $i$ passing below its midpoint and the label $i+1$ above. Together with
the first-under-second stacking convention of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]] this fixes the sign
convention for every signed crossing on this page and its companion.

**The opposite half twist.** The **opposite** (clockwise) half twist at $i$ is
defined by the reflected path

$$\rho^{-}(t):=\bigl(\rho_1(t),-\rho_2(t)\bigr),$$

through the motions $(\sigma_i^{-})_i(t):=m_i+\rho^{-}(t)$,
$(\sigma_i^{-})_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho^{-}(t)$ and
$(\sigma_i^{-})_k(t):=q_k$ for $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$. It is again a braid supported
in $U_i$ with endpoint permutation the transposition of $i$ and $i+1$; its pair
turns through the same half turn clockwise, the label $i$ passing above the
midpoint. The two motions are not equal, and they are not related by a
reparametrisation of the height: they are the two signed crossings of the pair.

**The opposite motion is the group inverse.** For a braid $\beta$ the reversed
braid $\overline\beta_j(t)=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)$ represents
$[\beta]^{-1}$ in the group $G_n$
([[thm-geometric-braids-form-a-group]]). For $\beta=\sigma_i$ one computes
$\overline{\sigma_i}=\sigma_i^{-}$: reversing the height and relabelling by the
transposition of $i$ and $i+1$ sends $\rho(t)=m_i+(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ to the
motion with relative path $-\rho(1-t)$, which is the reflected path
$\rho^-$ traversed from $t=0$ to $t=1$. Hence

$$[\sigma_i^{-}]=[\sigma_i]^{-1}\qquad\text{in }G_n .$$

**Elementary cases.** For $n\le1$ there is no index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$,
and there are no elementary half twists; the assertions above are vacuous. For
$n\ge2$ and $1\le i\le n-1$ both $[\sigma_i]$ and $[\sigma_i^{-}]$ are
nonidentity elements of $G_n$, since their endpoint permutations are
transpositions, which are not the identity permutation.

**Two letters do not commute in general.** For adjacent indices the supports
$U_i$ and $U_{i+1}$ overlap and no commutation is asserted;
[[lem-geometric-far-commutativity]] proves commutativity only for disjoint
supports.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]]. Write

$$G_n:=\{[\beta]:\beta\ \text{a braid based at}\ Q\}$$

for the set of braid isotopy classes relative to the top and bottom
([[def-braid-isotopy-relative-top-and-bottom]]), and let $[\gamma][\beta]:
=[\gamma\star\beta]$ be the stacking of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]]. Then:

**(a)** $G_n$ is a group ([[def-group]]) with this operation. Its identity is
the class $[e]$ of the trivial braid $e_j(t):=q_j$, and the inverse of
$[\beta]$, for $\beta=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ with endpoint permutation $\pi(\beta)$,
is the class of the **reversed braid**

$$\overline\beta_j(t):=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)\qquad(t\in I,\ 1\le j\le n).$$

**(b)** The endpoint permutation map

$$\pi\colon G_n\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad[\beta]\longmapsto\pi(\beta),$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]).

The construction is choice-free: all motions and reparametrisations used are
given by explicit formulas.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $\beta=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a geometric braid with
the fixed real basepoints $q_j=((2j-n-1)/(4(n+1)),0)$ and endpoint
permutation $\pi$, as in [[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]].
Identify the disk with $\{x\in\mathbb C:|x|<1\}$ and put
$$V=(D^\circ\times[0,1])/((x,1)\sim(x,0)).$$
The quotient and its topology use [[def-product-topology]] and the circle
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of [[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]].
The interval images
$$s_j=\{[(z_j(t),t)]:0\le t\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\beta)=\bigcup_{j=1}^n s_j$$
are the **closure in the open solid torus**. In general an individual
$s_j$ is an interval image, not a closed circle: its last point is the
first point of $s_{\pi(j)}$.

**Components and orientation.** For a cycle
$(j,\pi(j),\ldots,\pi^{k-1}(j))$ concatenate these $k$ strand maps in
that order, with parameter in $[0,k]$. Their endpoints agree in $V$,
so the concatenation factors through $\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$.
It is injective on this circle: points at distinct nonintegral heights
can agree only when their parameters have the same fractional part,
and the distinct strands at that height have distinct disk coordinates;
at integral heights only the specified adjacent endpoints agree.
Thus each cycle gives an embedded circle. Different cycles give
disjoint circles, and every strand belongs to exactly one cycle.
These circles are precisely the connected components of the closure.
The orientation is increasing concatenation parameter. In particular
the number of components equals the number of cycles of $\pi$.

**The standard axis and fixed framing.** In
$S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, as in
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], set
$$A=\{(0,w):|w|=1\},\qquad P_\theta=\{(z,w)\in S^3:z\ne0,\ \arg z=\theta\}.$$
Fix the following particular diffeomorphism, including its disk framing:
$$\varphi([(x,t)])=  \bigl(\sqrt{1-|x|^2}\,e^{2\pi it},x\bigr):  V\longrightarrow S^3\setminus A.$$
Its inverse has disk coordinate $x=w$ and circle coordinate
$[t]=[\arg z/(2\pi)]$. Every $P_\theta$ is consequently an open disk.
The **raw topological oriented closure** is
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{top}}=\varphi(\operatorname{cl}(\beta)).$$
This explicit $\varphi$ is part of the construction; the definition
does not allow an arbitrary page-preserving change of framing.

**Page intersections and smooth representatives.** The whole closure
meets every page in exactly $n$ points. A component belonging to a
$\pi$-cycle of length $k$ meets each page in exactly $k$ points:
at any fractional height it uses exactly those $k$ distinct strands.
The page coordinate of its concatenation is $[t]$, for
$t\in\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$, so its oriented degree is $+k$.
If all disk-coordinate strand maps are smooth and have all positive-order derivatives
zero at their endpoints, their cycle concatenations have matching jets
at every seam. The page coordinate has nonzero derivative, so the
result is a smooth embedding of disjoint oriented circles, in the
sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. For an endpoint-flat smooth braid, its literal $\varphi$-image is therefore a smooth oriented link and is denoted $\widehat\beta$.

**Closure in the smooth oriented-link category.** The raw image need not be smooth, even if individual strands are smooth but their endpoint jets fail to match at the cycle seams. For an arbitrary continuous braid, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) and choose a smooth representative $\beta_s$ by [[lem-every-geometric-braid-is-braid-isotopic-to-a-smooth-braid]]. Make it endpoint-flat by composing all disk-coordinate strands with a fixed smooth nondecreasing $\psi:I\to I$, equal to $0$ near $0$ and $1$ near $1$. Interpolation of height maps $(1-u)t+u\psi(t)$ is an endpoint-fixed braid isotopy, because every strand is evaluated at the same height. The smooth-category closure of $\beta$ is the oriented-link isotopy class of this chosen model's literal $\varphi$-image; when a subset is needed, use that chosen closed-braid representative. Independence of the representative is proved by [[lem-closure-depends-only-on-the-braid-isotopy-class]]. Page and cycle properties refer to the chosen constructed closed braid, with the same number of strands and endpoint permutation as $\beta$.

If $\beta$ already has smooth strands with matching cycle-seam jets, in particular if it is endpoint-flat, its literal raw image is a smooth link and is retained as $\widehat\beta$. The raw quotient, fixed $\varphi$, finite cycles, page counts and trivial closures remain choice-free. Finite elementary words have explicit smooth endpoint-flat models, so forming their literal closures also requires no choice assumption; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used for the general continuous-representative convention and its independence theorem.

**The trivial closure.** For the constant braid its circles are
$\{(\sqrt{1-q_j^2}e^{2\pi it},q_j):[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\}$.
They are latitudes of the sphere
$S=\{(z,w)\in S^3:\operatorname{Im}w=0\}$, with
$\operatorname{Re}w=q_j$. Each northern cap
$C_j=\{p\in S:\operatorname{Re}w(p)\ge q_j\}$ is a smooth disk:
stereographic coordinates on $S$ give radius
$\sqrt{(1-q_j)/(1+q_j)}$ for this cap. To make their spanning disks
disjoint, let $e$ be the unit vector in the $\operatorname{Im}w$
direction, set $\varepsilon=\pi/16$ and
$f_j(p)=\varepsilon(\operatorname{Re}w(p)-q_j)$ on $C_j$, and use
$$F_j(p)=\cos(f_j(p))p+\sin(f_j(p))e.$$
The boundary is fixed. The tubular parametrization
$(p,s)\mapsto\cos(s)p+\sin(s)e$ is injective for $|s|<\pi/2$,
and $0\le f_j<\pi/8$. On overlapping caps, if $q_i<q_j$ then
$f_i-f_j=\varepsilon(q_j-q_i)>0$, so their graphs are disjoint.
Thus these are pairwise disjoint smooth spanning disks. The trivial
$n$-braid closes to the oriented $n$-component unlink; for $n=1$
this is the unknot.

At $n=0$ all strand and cycle unions are empty, every page has zero intersections,
and the closure is the empty link. The basepoint list and disk constructions
above then have no entries.

derivations.claim: The endpoint permutation of $(\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1})^2$ is $(12)(23)(12)(23)=(1\ 3\ 2)$, because each half twist has the adjacent transposition as endpoint permutation and inverse has the same transposition. By [F8], its closure is one component. Cut the standard four-crossing figure-eight diagram along its projection regions and four crossing arcs. Above and below the diagram this produces two ideal balls: each crossing arc has four face-side copies, and every face is a diagram region. Gluing upper and lower faces with the same region label restores the cut-open complement, because each cut face and crossing-arc side is identified with exactly its original mate; the only unfilled points are the deleted knot arcs, which are ideal vertices. Collapsing the two bigon faces gives two tetrahedra. Recording the vertex matches on their four faces gives exactly the four maps in the statement.

By [F2], at $z_1=z_2=z_3=w_1=w_2=w_3=\omega$ every edge parameter is $\omega$. The first edge class has product $\omega^6=1$, and the second has product $\omega^6=1$; each class contains six edge copies, so its total dihedral angle is $6(\pi/3)=2\pi$.

Applying the four vertex maps identifies all eight tetrahedron vertices into one ideal vertex and the twelve tetrahedron edges into the two six-edge classes in the statement. To check the link vertices explicitly, write $u|v$ for the truncation corner at ideal vertex $u$ on edge $uv$. The four corner classes are $\{0|1,0|2,3|2,3'|1',3'|2',0'|1'\}$, $\{1|0,1'|3',2|0,2'|3',1'|0',2|3\}$, $\{1|2,1'|2',0|3,0'|2',1|3,0'|3'\}$, and $\{2|1,2'|1',3|0,2'|0',3|1,3'|0'\}$; these are disjoint and contain all $24$ link corners. The eight link triangles have their $24$ sides identified in $12$ pairs, so $\chi=4-12+8=0$. The four face maps give a connected adjacency graph on the eight link triangles; their induced boundary-orientation signs are respectively negative, negative, negative, negative. Hence the link is connected, closed and orientable, and therefore is a torus.

Tracking the stated eight-triangle strip across the four face pairings closes each listed path. Cut the strip open along $\alpha$: the $\beta$ path becomes an arc joining the two copies of that cut, and the face table shows it crosses the cut once, from the negative to the positive side. Thus the single signed intersection is $+1$; on a torus this makes $([\alpha],[\beta])$ a homology basis. Since $\pi_1(T)=\mathbb Z^2$ and its abelianization is $H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$, these loops also generate $\pi_1(T)$. Substituting the regular shape into the listed corner products gives $H(\alpha)=((\omega\omega)/(\omega\omega))^2=1$ and $H(\beta)=\omega/\omega=1$.

The edge conditions in step 1.2, torus link in step 2.1, and basis cusp multipliers in step 3.1 satisfy [F3], so the glued metric is complete at its unique torus cusp. The face maps are hyperbolic face isometries; the $2\pi$ edge-angle sums make the metric smooth across every edge, and the only omitted locus is the single ideal vertex. Thus completeness at this cusp is completeness of the whole glued complement. Each tetrahedron has volume $v_3$ by [F5], so additivity gives total volume $2v_3<\infty$; its horospherical cusp truncation also has finite volume by [F4]. The induced metric on the figure-eight complement is therefore complete and finite-volume with one peripheral torus cusp.

Define the standard figure-eight knot $K_8$ to be the oriented closure of the three-strand geometric braid $(\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1})^2$. Its endpoint permutation is a $3$-cycle, so this closure has one component.

Let $\Delta_0=[0,1,2,3]$ and $\Delta_1=[0',1',2',3']$ be oriented ideal tetrahedra with orientation-reversing affine face maps
$$
[0,1,2]\to[3',1',2'],\quad
[0,1,3]\to[0',1',2'],\quad
[0,2,3]\to[0',1',3'],\quad
[1,2,3]\to[0',2',3'].
$$
This is the two-tetrahedron ideal triangulation obtained from the standard four-crossing figure-eight diagram by cutting along crossing arcs, identifying upper and lower polyhedron faces with equal region labels, and collapsing the two bigon faces. Its edge classes are
$$
\{01,02,23,0'1',1'3',2'3'\},\qquad
\{12,03,13,1'2',0'2',0'3'\};
$$
each has valence six, and the unique ideal vertex link is a torus. Put shape $z_1$ on $01,23$, shape $z_2$ on $03,12$, and shape $z_3$ on $02,13$ in $\Delta_0$; put shape $w_1$ on $0'1',2'3'$, shape $w_2$ on $0'3',1'2'$, and shape $w_3$ on $0'2',1'3'$ in $\Delta_1$. Unfold the eight cusp-link triangles by the face maps into the standard rectangular strip, and label them $a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h$ from left to right; identify the strip boundary sides as prescribed by those same maps. Let $\alpha$ be the edge path across the strip from the left side of $a$ on the left boundary to the left side of $a$ on the right boundary, and let $\beta$ be the edge path on the left boundary from the base of $a$ to the top of $h$. Their ordered corner factors are respectively $z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1},z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1}$ and $z_2^{-1},w_1$. The face-pairing incidence check gives one positive transverse intersection, so their homology classes form a basis of $H_1$ and the loops form a basis of $\pi_1$ of the torus link. The two edge products are $z_1^2z_3w_1^2w_3$ and $z_2^2z_3w_2^2w_3$, while
$$
H(\alpha)=\left(\frac{z_2z_3}{w_2w_3}\right)^2,\qquad H(\beta)=\frac{w_1}{z_2}.
$$
For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, assigning $z_1=z_2=z_3=w_1=w_2=w_3=\omega$ makes both edge products and both cusp multipliers equal to $1$ and gives total angle $2\pi$ around each edge. The gluing therefore gives the figure-eight complement a complete finite-volume curvature $-1$ metric with one peripheral torus cusp.

Every regular ideal tetrahedron in hyperbolic three-space has volume
$$
v_3=3\Lambda(\pi/3)
=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).
$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ and $N$ be interiors of compact connected oriented knot exteriors carrying complete finite-volume hyperbolic metrics. Every isomorphism $\pi_1(M)\to\pi_1(N)$, considered up to the conjugacy induced by basepoint changes, is realized by a unique isometry in the corresponding proper homotopy class. If the isomorphism is induced by an orientation-preserving proper homotopy equivalence, the isometry preserves orientation. In particular, the two metrics have equal volume, where volume is the integral of their Riemannian volume densities.

For every real $\theta$, $\Lambda$ is continuous, odd, and $\pi$-periodic, with $\Lambda(\pi/2)=0$ and
$$
\Lambda(2\theta)=2\Lambda(\theta)+2\Lambda(\theta+\pi/2).
$$
For $0\le\theta\le\pi$,
$$
\Lambda(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sin(2n\theta)}{n^2}.
$$
In particular,
$$
\Lambda(\pi/3)=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).
$$
For every integer $N\ge1$, the positive remainder after the terms $k=0,\ldots,N$ is at most $\sqrt3/(72N^2)$.

For $N=10{,}000$ and $Q=10^{30}$, let $a_k=\lfloor Q/(3k+1)^2\rfloor$ and $b_k=\lfloor Q/(3k+2)^2\rfloor$. Exact integer division gives $781302412526189990283977435641\le\sum_{k=0}^{N}(a_k-b_k-1)\le Q\sum_{k=0}^{N}((3k+1)^{-2}-(3k+2)^{-2})\le\sum_{k=0}^{N}(a_k-b_k+1)=781302412526189990283977455643$. Also $r=1732050807568877293527446341505<Q\sqrt3<r+1=1732050807568877293527446341506$, as verified by squaring both integer endpoints against $3Q^2$. The truncated volume is $V_N=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}\sum_{k=0}^{N}((3k+1)^{-2}-(3k+2)^{-2})$, because [F3] gives $\Lambda(\pi/3)=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}$ times that series. The preceding integer bounds and $r<Q\sqrt3<r+1$ give $\frac{3r(781302412526189990283977435641)}{2Q^2}\le V_N\le\frac{3(r+1)(781302412526189990283977455643)}{2Q^2}$. Exact cross-multiplication places $V_N$ between $2.02988321185$ and $2.02988321187$. Its omitted positive tail is less than $1.445\times10^{-9}$ because $6\sqrt3/(72N^2)=\sqrt3/(12N^2)<1.445\times10^{-9}$. Thus the complete interval lies strictly between $2.029875$ and $2.029885$, giving the stated five-decimal rounding.

Steps 1.1–2.1 compute the volume of the explicit complete gluing metric. For any other complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric on the same exterior interior, the identity fundamental-group isomorphism satisfies [F4], which supplies a volume-preserving isometry. Therefore the computed value is independent of the chosen complete hyperbolic metric and is the asserted complete hyperbolic volume of the figure-eight complement.

Use the upper half-space model

\mathbb H^3=\{(x+iy,t):x,y\in\mathbb R,\ t>0\},\qquad
ds^2=t^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2+dt^2),
$$
whose ideal boundary is $\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$. An oriented ideal tetrahedron in normalized position has ideal vertices $0,1,\infty,z$, where $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Its three edge-shape parameters are
$$
z,\qquad z'=\frac1{1-z},\qquad z''=\frac{z-1}{z},
$$
each assigned to one pair of opposite edges; the parameter at a corner of a truncated ideal vertex triangle is the parameter of the incident edge. For an oriented path $\gamma$ in a triangulated torus link of ideal vertices, its cusp multiplier $H(\gamma)$ is the product of the corner parameters encountered along $\gamma$, using the parameter when the path cuts off that corner on its left and its reciprocal when it cuts off the corner on its right.

For an oriented ideal tetrahedron with normalized vertices $0,1,\infty,z$ and $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its three edge-shape parameters are $z$, $z'=1/(1-z)$, and $z''=(z-1)/z$. They satisfy $zz'z''=-1$, and their arguments in $(0,\pi)$ are the three dihedral angles, whose sum is $\pi$. For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, the choice $z=\omega$ gives $z=z'=z''=\omega$ and all six dihedral angles equal to $\pi/3$.

Let an orientable finite ideal triangulation have exactly one ideal vertex, whose link is a torus. Suppose its tetrahedra carry positive shapes whose edge products equal $1$ and whose dihedral angles sum to $2\pi$ around every edge. If the cusp multipliers $H(\alpha)$ and $H(\beta)$ are $1$ for a basis $\alpha,\beta$ of the torus fundamental group, then the glued hyperbolic metric is complete at that cusp.

Let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb C$ be a rank-two lattice acting on $\mathbb H^3$ by horizontal translations, and let
$$
C=\{(x+iy,t):t\ge1\}/\Gamma
$$
be the quotient of the horoball $t\ge1$. If $A$ is the Euclidean area of a fundamental parallelogram for $\Gamma$, then the end is at infinite hyperbolic distance and $\operatorname{Vol}(C)=A/2$.

A compact orientable three-manifold $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. A properly embedded surface is **incompressible** if it admits no embedded disk whose interior misses the surface and whose boundary is an essential simple closed curve in it. A boundary subsurface is **$\pi_1$-injective** if the inclusion of each component induces an injection on fundamental groups. A **pared pair** is a pair $(M,P)$ in which $M$ is compact, orientable and irreducible, and $P$ is a possibly empty compact subsurface of $\partial M$ whose pairwise disjoint components are $\pi_1$-injective annuli or tori, every noncyclic abelian subgroup of $\pi_1(M)$ is conjugate into $\pi_1$ of a component of $P$ up to base-path conjugacy, and every map of pairs
$$
(S^1\times I,S^1\times\partial I)\longrightarrow(M,P)
$$
that induces injections on fundamental groups is homotopic through maps of pairs into $P$, so its boundary remains in $P$ during the homotopy. Write $\partial_0M=\partial M\setminus\operatorname{int}P$. A **horoball** is a region bounded by a horosphere, a Euclidean plane or sphere tangent to the ideal boundary at one point. The **peripheral subgroup** for a component of $P$ is the image of its fundamental group in $\pi_1(M)$, recorded up to conjugacy. A **hyperbolic structure** on $(M,P)$ is a curvature $-1$ metric on $\operatorname{int}M$ described by an atlas of charts into $\mathbb H^3$ whose transition maps are in $\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$. Its developing map $\operatorname{dev}$ from the universal cover and holonomy homomorphism $\rho:\pi_1(M)\to\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$ satisfy $\operatorname{dev}(gx)=\rho(g)\operatorname{dev}(x)$. The metric is **complete** when it is geodesically complete. A **cusp** corresponding to a component of $P$ is a quotient of a horoball by the associated peripheral subgroup. derivations.claim: For each tetrahedron, [F1] supplies a nondegenerate ideal simplex, and the assigned face maps are hyperbolic isometries because their three corresponding ideal vertices have the same cross-ratio shape. Around a finite edge, the product equation makes the accumulated complex similarity the identity, while the angle sum $2\pi$ makes the total rotation one full turn. Thus the simplices glue to a smooth curvature $-1$ metric away from the ideal vertices.

Fix an ideal vertex $v$ and let $T_v$ be its torus link. Truncate the corners at $v$ by small horospheres. The resulting finite collection of Euclidean corner triangles triangulates $T_v$, and the face identifications restrict to Euclidean similarities. At a vertex of this link triangulation, corresponding to an incident edge of the ideal triangulation, the edge-shape product equation makes the accumulated complex similarity equal to $1$, while the $2\pi$ angle sum makes the total cone angle exactly $2\pi$. Thus the link similarity structure has no cone singularities. For a loop $\gamma$ on $T_v$, the linear part of its similarity holonomy is the multiplier $H_v(\gamma)$: crossing a corner contributes its shape factor or reciprocal according to the side traversed. The two assumed basis multipliers are $1$, so this linear part is the identity for every loop in $\pi_1(T_v)$.

Fix a Euclidean metric in one link chart and transport it through the similarity charts. The metric is independent of the transport path, because every loop has identity linear holonomy and translations preserve the Euclidean metric. This gives a global flat metric $g_v$ on the compact torus $T_v$, hence a complete one. Its lift to the universal cover is complete as well: any geodesic projects to a geodesic on the complete torus, extends there, and the extension lifts through the covering. The lifted Euclidean charts develop to a local isometry into $\mathbb R^2$. Every finite straight segment starting at a point in the image lifts to its endpoint: a partial lift has finite length, is therefore Cauchy, and extends from its limit by the local isometry. Hence the development is onto. For a small Euclidean ball about any point, lifting its radial segments from each preimage gives disjoint isometric copies of that ball; lifting the reverse radial segments shows these copies exhaust its preimage. Thus the development is a covering, and since $\mathbb R^2$ is simply connected it is an isometry. Deck transformations have identity linear part by the trivial link holonomy, so act by translations. Compactness of $T_v$ makes their translation vectors a rank-two lattice $\Lambda_v$. The assembled end is therefore the quotient of a horoball by $\Lambda_v$, with metric $dr^2+e^{-2r}g_v$ in horospherical depth $r$. A path escaping toward the ideal vertex has length at least the change in $r$, so the end is complete. Repeating this argument at each of the finitely many vertices proves completeness at every end. This is the local cusp argument underlying [F3], carried out separately on every link; the one-vertex Statement of [F3] is not applied to the full triangulation.

A horospherical truncation of each ideal tetrahedron is compact and has finite volume because its smooth hyperbolic volume density is bounded on that compact region. Each removed vertex tail is contained in a rank-two horocusp and has finite volume by [F4]. There are finitely many tetrahedra and vertices, so the glued manifold has finite total volume.

The part remaining after all cusp neighborhoods are removed is a compact union of truncated tetrahedra. Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence. If infinitely many terms lie in that compact part, a subsequence converges there and the Cauchy property forces the whole sequence to the same limit. Otherwise the sequence eventually lies in the union of the finitely many disjoint cusp ends; sufficiently deep points in distinct ends have positive separation through the compact core, so the Cauchy property forces it eventually into one end, where it converges by step 2.1. Thus the full metric is complete. Together with step 3.1 and the curvature $-1$ charts from step 1.1, this is a complete finite-volume hyperbolic structure as defined in [F5].

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Define the standard figure-eight knot $K_8$ to be the oriented closure of the three-strand geometric braid $(\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1})^2$. Its endpoint permutation is a $3$-cycle, so this closure has one component.

Let $\Delta_0=[0,1,2,3]$ and $\Delta_1=[0',1',2',3']$ be oriented ideal tetrahedra with orientation-reversing affine face maps
$$
[0,1,2]\to[3',1',2'],\quad
[0,1,3]\to[0',1',2'],\quad
[0,2,3]\to[0',1',3'],\quad
[1,2,3]\to[0',2',3'].
$$
This is the two-tetrahedron ideal triangulation obtained from the standard four-crossing figure-eight diagram by cutting along crossing arcs, identifying upper and lower polyhedron faces with equal region labels, and collapsing the two bigon faces. Its edge classes are
$$
\{01,02,23,0'1',1'3',2'3'\},\qquad
\{12,03,13,1'2',0'2',0'3'\};
$$
each has valence six, and the unique ideal vertex link is a torus. Put shape $z_1$ on $01,23$, shape $z_2$ on $03,12$, and shape $z_3$ on $02,13$ in $\Delta_0$; put shape $w_1$ on $0'1',2'3'$, shape $w_2$ on $0'3',1'2'$, and shape $w_3$ on $0'2',1'3'$ in $\Delta_1$. Unfold the eight cusp-link triangles by the face maps into the standard rectangular strip, and label them $a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h$ from left to right; identify the strip boundary sides as prescribed by those same maps. Let $\alpha$ be the edge path across the strip from the left side of $a$ on the left boundary to the left side of $a$ on the right boundary, and let $\beta$ be the edge path on the left boundary from the base of $a$ to the top of $h$. Their ordered corner factors are respectively $z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1},z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1}$ and $z_2^{-1},w_1$. The face-pairing incidence check gives one positive transverse intersection, so their homology classes form a basis of $H_1$ and the loops form a basis of $\pi_1$ of the torus link. The two edge products are $z_1^2z_3w_1^2w_3$ and $z_2^2z_3w_2^2w_3$, while
$$
H(\alpha)=\left(\frac{z_2z_3}{w_2w_3}\right)^2,\qquad H(\beta)=\frac{w_1}{z_2}.
$$
For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, assigning $z_1=z_2=z_3=w_1=w_2=w_3=\omega$ makes both edge products and both cusp multipliers equal to $1$ and gives total angle $2\pi$ around each edge. The gluing therefore gives the figure-eight complement a complete finite-volume curvature $-1$ metric with one peripheral torus cusp.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K_8$ be the standard figure-eight knot with compact exterior obtained by deleting the binding neighborhood from its open-book presentation and peripheral basis $(\mu,\lambda)$, where $\mu$ is the positive meridian and $\lambda$ is the preferred zero-homology longitude. The exterior fibers over $S^1$ with fiber a once-punctured torus and monodromy fixing its boundary pointwise. Filling along the slope $\lambda$ produces a torus bundle over $S^1$. For the fiber and ordered core basis in the figure-eight plumbing convention, the induced action on the capped torus homology is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $M$ is a closed connected orientable three-manifold with a complete Riemannian metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$, then its fundamental group contains no subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$.

Let $\overline M$ be a compact connected oriented three-manifold whose boundary is a disjoint union of tori $T_1,\ldots,T_k$. Choose an ordered integral basis $([\mu_i],[\lambda_i])$ for each $H_1(T_i;\mathbb Z)$. A **slope** on $T_i$ is an unoriented isotopy class of essential simple closed curves whose homology class is $p_i[\mu_i]+q_i[\lambda_i]$ for a primitive pair $(p_i,q_i)\in\mathbb Z^2$; simultaneous negation gives the same unoriented slope. The primitive-pair correspondence gives exactly one such slope for each primitive pair modulo sign. The **ordinary Dehn filling** along a tuple of slopes indexed by $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ attaches an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to each $T_i$, $i\in J$, by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{*\}]$ to the chosen slope. The gluing maps are part of the filling data; $i\notin J$ means that the cusp is left unfilled, denoted by the parameter $\infty$.

For a hyperbolic deformation, the **generalized cone-filling parameter space** at each cusp is the one-point compactification $\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$ of the real coefficient plane, with $\infty$ denoting the complete cusp. A primitive integral pair $(p_i,q_i)$ is an ordinary smooth filling coefficient. If a realized generalized parameter lies on the ray $g_i=r_i(p_i,q_i)$ with $r_i>0$ and $(p_i,q_i)$ primitive integral, its topological core direction is the ordinary slope $(p_i,q_i)$ and its cone angle is $2\pi/r_i$. Only $r_i=1$ is the ordinary smooth filling; $r_i>1$ describes a cone or orbifold completion and does not turn the nonprimitive vector $g_i$ into a slope.

A **covering map** is a continuous surjection $p:E\to B$ such that every $b\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ for which $p^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets $V_j$, called **sheets**, and each restriction $p|_{V_j}:V_j\to U$ is a homeomorphism ([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]], [[def-disjoint-union-topology]]). Such a $U$ is **evenly covered**, and $p^{-1}(b)$ is the **fibre** over $b$. A covering is **trivial** when it is isomorphic over $B$ to a product projection $B\times F\to B$ with $F$ discrete.
For a covering $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$, the induced homomorphism $p_*:\pi_1(E,e_0)\to\pi_1(B,b_0)$ is injective.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for the chosen smooth knot-exterior data. Let $K_8$ be the standard figure-eight knot, presented as the boundary of the square plumbing of one positive and one negative Hopf band, with one boundary component. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose positive normal push-off of its core has linking number $+1$ with the core; a negative Hopf band has linking number $-1$. A square plumbing identifies a square in the boundary collars of the annuli with the four boundary edges alternating between the annuli, then smooths corners. Let $F$ be this plumbed surface, and choose the compact exterior by deleting the interior of the binding neighborhood $N(K_8)\cong\partial F\times D^2$ supplied by the open book; on every page this neighborhood meets the page in an annular collar of $\partial F$. Let $a,b$ be the core curves, ordered so that $a$ is the positive-band core and $a\cdot_F b=+1$. The exterior $E_{K_8}$ fibers over $S^1$ with fiber $F$. With the twist convention that the positive twist $R_a$ sends $a\mapsto a$, $b\mapsto a+b$, and the negative twist $L_b$ sends $a\mapsto a+b$, $b\mapsto b$, the monodromy is $R_a\circ L_b$. After capping $\partial F$ by a disk, its action on the ordered homology basis $([a],[b])$ is represented by $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

derivations.claim: First identify the two figure-eight models used here. In [F3], $K_8$ is the closure of $(\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1})^2$, the standard four-crossing figure-eight diagram. In [F9], the same standard figure-eight knot is presented as the boundary of the square plumbing of a positive and a negative Hopf band; Calegari's Example 5.39 identifies the boundary of the opposite-handed Hopf-band Murasugi sum as the figure-eight knot. Thus both are the same oriented $4_1$ knot class, and an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy identifies the braid closure with the plumbing boundary. Choose the binding and tubular neighborhoods compatibly under this isotopy. It identifies the compact exteriors and carries the positive meridian and preferred longitude to the corresponding peripheral classes (up to simultaneous reversal, which does not change the unoriented zero slope). The hyperbolic exterior from [F3] and the fibered exterior from [F9] are therefore the same marked exterior for this example. By [A1] and [F2], the countable-choice premise [F1] holds. The face gluing and regular-shape assignment in [F3] give the complete finite-volume metric and its two-tetrahedron volume. By [F4] and [F6], the zero filling along the preferred longitude is the stated torus bundle.

Write the bundle as the mapping torus of its torus monodromy. Pull it back along the explicit universal cover $t\mapsto e^{2\pi i t}$ of $S^1$; its total space is $T^2\times\mathbb R$, and the pullback projection is a covering because it is trivial over each lifted bundle chart. Its fundamental group is $\pi_1(T^2)\cong\mathbb Z^2$. By [F8], this subgroup injects into the fundamental group of the filled manifold.

If the filled manifold admitted a complete hyperbolic metric, it would be a closed connected three-manifold with curvature $-1$. By [F5] its fundamental group could contain no $\mathbb Z^2$ subgroup, contradicting step 2.1. Hence the zero filling is nonhyperbolic.
